World.title: Regional emergency departments a 'basket case of mania', doctor warns
World.content:
Victoria's most dysfunctional and dangerous emergency departments are in regional areas, health department data shows.

The quarterly statistics on the state's public hospitals include tracking of emergency department (ED) stays 24 hours or longer, an indicator of pressure on hospital resources.

There were about 3,300 patients across the state admitted to emergency from January to March this year who stayed there for at least 24 hours.

Of these patients, 2,330 patients, or 70 per cent, were in regional and rural hospitals, with the highest numbers in Ballarat, Albury (which services many Victorians) and Bendigo.

By comparison, between January and March 2025, 1,900 patients stayed 24 hours or more in Victorian EDs.

Of these, 1,300, or 69 per cent, were in regional and rural hospitals.

The health department's performance target is zero patients spending more than 24 hours in the ED.

A report by the Victorian Auditor-General's Office from 2024 said the health department set that target in 2011, along with a goal of 81 per cent of all emergency patients staying in an ED for four hours or less.

The report noted the goal had been "consistently missed" and that in 10 years from 2013 to 2023 there had been a "significant increase in the number of patients exceeding a 24-hour stay".

Doctors on the ground in some of the state's worst-performing EDs in regional Victoria say unsustainable levels of pressure on staff are the new normal, and it is affecting patient safety.

From today, public hospital doctors statewide are starting industrial action over pay and conditions.

In regional Victoria, doctors can choose from a variety of measures such as not responding to work-related emails from hospital management and displaying campaign material as part of the industrial action.

Multiple ED staff have spoken to the ABC about their concerns on the condition of anonymity, for fear of losing their jobs.

Patients wait 40 hours

Ballarat Base Hospital ED doctor David* said patients having to wait more than 40 hours in ED for a bed on the ward "wasn't uncommon".

He said it was normal for ED patients to overflow into corridors or unmonitored waiting rooms, where there was a risk they could deteriorate.

David says he feels "defeated" by his job and is considering leaving medicine. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

"I've seen people who have waited in this waiting room then require emergency surgery," David said.

The doctor said he had seen stroke patients being treated in the corridor in full view of others, depriving them of dignity.

David said another doctor had told him of a recent incident where an intern assessed a patient as having a headache and gave them pain relief.

The patient then suffered a bleed to the brain.

"Often because of how busy it is, [senior doctors] don't get to lay eyes on that patient … they're just trusting what is said [by a junior]," David said.

"Should the intern have that much pressure to see patients independently? Of course not.

"Everyone's doing the best to cope in a system that is like a pressure cooker.

"We're understaffed, underfunded."

David said he felt "defeated" by his job and was considering leaving medicine.

Another Ballarat ED doctor described the emergency department as a "basket case of mania" while yet another ED doctor said management's efforts to address staff burnout in the Ballarat ED were misguided.

"We don't need someone to tell us how to identify burnout. We're the literal definition of burnout," they said.

No privacy

Kevin Harper has worked in the healthcare industry for more than 40 years, and has visited ED departments regularly with his partner, who has a long-term health condition.

Kevin Harper says there are potential privacy issues if people are being treated in open areas. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

Mr Harper said the Ballarat ED has not grown in size to accommodate the growing population.

"I heard the senior nurse discussing with one of the triage staff where they could possibly put beds into corridors to make them not just a waiting space, but a treatment space as well," he said.

" So you're hearing confidential information being discussed, bloods are being taken, ECGs all in the corridor without any curtains or privacy at all. "

A Grampians Health spokesperson acknowledged "some patients who require admission to [Ballarat Base] hospital may experience extended waits for an inpatient bed".

"The safety of patients and staff is our highest priority," the spokesperson said.

"We will never turn anyone away, so when we experience periods of extremely high demand, there may not be a bed or private bay immediately available."

The spokesperson said population growth was "contributing to increased demand for healthcare services" and noted that the "pressures" in the Ballarat ED "reflect broader challenges being felt across healthcare systems nationally".

"Sustained pressure on the healthcare system can be challenging for our workforce," the spokesperson said.

"Supporting our workforce remains a key priority, and we continue to invest in staff wellbeing initiatives and workforce development."

'Who's going to die first?'

At Albury Hospital, which treats a lot of Victorians from the state's north-east region, an ED clinician said there was a constant worry about "who's going to die first?".

An ED clinician at Albury Hospital says sometimes it feels like a "war zone". (ABC Goulburn Murray: Annie Brown)

"You're gambling with the next decision that you make," the clinician said.

"You can't meet all the needs of everyone who's asking for help and it does feel like a war zone at times.

"[There's] definitely a feeling of helplessness.

"We're in constant need of beds."

It was a similar story at Mildura Base Hospital, according to a clinician who said patients often spent longer than 24 hours in ED.

They said it was common to treat patients in chairs and other temporary, non-private areas, and that junior doctors dealt with complex presentations with little or no supervision.

"I have enormous respect for the staff who keep trying to make the system work under this immense, sustained pressure," the clinician said.

"I do feel like it's getting more and more normalised, the level of strain these staff are getting."

An Albury Wodonga Health spokesperson said they recognised "that periods of increased demand place significant pressure on our workforce and would like to acknowledge the dedication, professionalism and resilience of our staff".

They said all patients "receive timely, high-quality emergency treatment to minimise time spent waiting".

Mildura Base Hospital has been contacted for comment.

A complete standstill

Warrnambool Base Hospital declared a code yellow from July 27 to 29, meaning the hospital was grappling with a sustained period of high demand.

Warrnambool Base Hospital had a code yellow towards the end of July. (ABC South West Victoria: Emily Bissland)

A health worker from the hospital said that during the internal escalation, many patients waited in the emergency department for more than 24 hours.

"It was a complete standstill," they said.

"There was one patient who had an entire three-day admission in our emergency observation unit.

"We usually try and get people out within four hours."

The worker said the intensive care unit was full at one point, and nurse-to-patient ratios were not being met.

"It's basically luck that nothing horrendous happened," they said.

The worker said the influx of patients was partly driven by a lack of doctor availability in the region, with some patients facing wait times of six weeks to see a GP.

The lack of available aged care spaces was also a factor, they said.

" People can't see GPs in the community to get their health under control, and they don't have nursing home beds to go to at the other end. "

The worker said they were concerned by the hospital's focus on moving people out of ED, as they believed it prioritised clearing space over patient care.

"It starts putting the focus on the wrong thing, because the shift goes from patient care and patient safety to getting people out, which is a dangerous mindset shift," they said.

The worker said healthcare staff bore the brunt of the increased demand on regional and rural hospitals, which was coupled with insufficient funding and resources.

"It literally breaks [healthcare workers], and that's going to be the next sort of crisis," they said.

South West Healthcare's chief operating officer Alex Demidov rejected the worker's claims.

"Patient care was not compromised at any point during the code yellow, our staffing was at full complement, and our intensive care unit operated at mandated nurse-to-patient ratios throughout," he said.

Long stays should be a 'never event'

Australian Medical Association (AMA) Victoria president Simon Judkins said ED stays of more than 24 hours disproportionately affected regional and rural hospitals, and it was "a real signal [of] a high level of dysfunction".

Simon Judkins says long emergency stays disproportionately affect regional areas. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"We don't see 24-hour stays at the Alfred [in Melbourne]," Dr Judkins said.

He said an eight-hour stay in an ED was a sign of a system under stress and operating over capacity.

"If you extrapolate that out to 24 hours that indicates a highly dysfunctional system," he said.

Dr Judkins said the AMA had worked with state and federal governments to classify an ED stay of 24 hours or more as a "never event".

"So, we're aiming for zero, and now we've got thousands of patients across the state," he said.

Dr Judkins said the lack of places to refer patients in regional areas, such as aged care homes, was exacerbating the ED problem.

"That whole system becomes log jammed, the hospital's filled up," Dr Judkins said.

"We don't have the beds, and that all just flows back, back into emergency department over-crowding and ambulances ramping."

Dr Judkins said he had heard recently Bendigo Hospital ED staff had turned up to work on a Monday morning to find 30 patients in the ED waiting for transfer to other wards.

"It guarantees that anybody who turns up with a stroke, anybody who turns up with a heart attack, anybody who turns up with a trauma, there'll be a delay to care," he said.

A spokesperson for Bendigo Health said it "continues to experience periods of high demand across our emergency and inpatient services".

"Our staff are working closely across the health service to manage patient flow and ensure patients receive the care they need as quickly and safely as possible," the spokesperson said.

AMA Victoria is calling on the state government to end "unsafe delays and improve transparency". (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

AMA Victoria calling for urgent intervention

AMA Victoria is calling on the state government to end "unsafe delays and improve transparency" in regional and rural hospitals, and to fund the modernisation of administrative systems in regional hospitals to help speed up processes.

"A lot of our regional hospitals still don't even have electronic medical records," Dr Judkins said.

The AMA also wants solutions to workforce shortages through investment in specialist training and gaps in access to care, and is calling for a parliamentary inquiry into regional and rural healthcare.

"It just seems it's a political football … and nobody's really come up with a long-term plan about how we're actually going to address it," he said.

Speaking to the ABC just before health minister Harriet Shing's recent resignation, Dr Judkins said she had listened to him "sometimes".

He was disappointed, he said, after sending Ms Shing a letter on July 9 about concerns with patient safety at Ballarat Base Hospital ED asking for her intervention.

He did not receive a response.

The state government said it was supporting Victoria's health service with "record investment and new solutions".

"We know how frustrating it is when faced with long ED wait time," a spokesperson said.

"During the busy winter flu season, Victorians should always consider alternative options like the Virtual Emergency Department or Urgent Care Clinics if their condition is not life-threatening."

World.title: Wind in the wilderness a real threat to unprepared hikers
World.content:
Urshla Connor knows from personal and professional experience that being prepared for changing winds and weather can be the difference between a beautiful bushwalk and a life-threatening situation in Tasmania.

In her role as a meteorologist with the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM), she regularly updates emergency services and the media on changing alpine conditions that often catch hikers unawares.

While she generates warnings and forecasts for the bureau's website and the BOM Weather app, Ms Connor always double-checks the latest information before starting a trek.

"Being a meteorologist, I probably check the weather more than most people," she said.

" I definitely plan my walks around the forecast. But on a multi-day walk in Tasmania, it's unrealistic to expect perfect weather every day. "

Urshla Connor says hikers should keep in mind that once they reach exposed ridgelines or summits, much stronger winds are a possibility. (Supplied: Urshla Connor)

Ms Connor said her most memorable experience of being caught in bad weather was on the Three Capes Track.

"We had two beautiful blue-sky days, but one day of cloud so thick we couldn't see 20 metres ahead, and winds so strong it felt like we'd be blown off Cape Pillar," she said.

" It reinforced that Tasmanian weather can be unforgiving. You have to carry the gear for the weather you're likely to get, not the weather you're hoping for. "

The weather in Tasmania can change quickly. (Unsplash: Lucas Canino)

Ms Connor cautioned that conditions can change extremely quickly in Tasmania and can be significantly different whether you're near the coast or up high on a mountain.

"Before you head out, it is important to check both the current observations and the forecast for the area you're planning to visit," she said.

"Search for your destination on the BOM Weather app or the bureau's website to compare the latest conditions with what's expected over the course of your walk, including temperature, wind and rainfall.

" Also keep an eye out for any Bushwalkers Weather Alerts, Severe Weather Warnings and Severe Thunderstorm Warnings affecting your area. "

Loading...

Bushwalkers should be aware that while air temperature generally decreases gradually with elevation, wind is often what makes exposed alpine areas significantly harsher.

"During winter, Tasmania is regularly affected by strong cold fronts from the Southern Ocean, bringing rapidly changing weather," Ms Connor said.

"As you gain elevation during these conditions, temperatures decrease, winds strengthen, and precipitation can become more intense."

She said most hikes begin in relatively sheltered locations, but "once you reach exposed ridgelines or summits, you're suddenly exposed to much stronger winds".

"Strong winds increase the rate at which your body loses heat — a phenomenon known as 'wind chill'," she said.

"Even when the air temperature isn't especially low, wind chill can increase the risk of cold stress and hypothermia, particularly in exposed alpine and coastal areas."

It is important to be prepared if hiking in Tasmania. (Unsplash: Creative Dummy llc)

Solo hiker's brush with danger on Overland Track A Tasmanian hiker has recounted her experience of misadventure while hiking in the state's rugged wilderness.

As winter sets in, many of Tasmania's peaks also receive snowfall.

Combined with strong winds, snow can reduce visibility, make tracks slippery and create freezing conditions that increase the risk of exposure.

"You can use the forecast maps to see how temperatures and wind speeds are expected to change along your route," Ms Connor said.

"Winds can significantly increase wind chill, so it's important to consider more than just the forecast temperature.

" That's why the bureau also provides an 'apparent' or 'feels like' temperature in its forecasts. For example, an air temperature of 6 degrees Celsius on Kunanyi/Mount Wellington can feel closer to -4C on a windy day. "

Urshla Connor says if she is out with people new to Tasmanian bushwalking, she will often carry spare gear "just in case". (Supplied: Urshla Connor)

Rescue statistics show that interstate visitors are far from the only ones being caught out by Tasmania's weather, with only 27 per cent of rescue operations involving mainland tourists.

In recent years, the rise of social media has inspired more people to explore Tasmania's wilderness, but not everyone is prepared for how quickly conditions can change.

"I've also learnt that not everyone knows what a proper rain jacket looks like," Ms Connor said.

"I've had friends turn up in fashionable spray jackets that look great, but aren't designed for hours of rain and strong winds.

"Now, if I'm walking with people who are new to Tasmanian bushwalking, I usually throw a couple of spare waterproof jackets and some extra gear in my pack, just in case."

The bureau continues to work closely with the Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service, and Tasmania Police Search and Rescue, to improve the weather information and warnings available to the community.

Urshla Connor and friends bushwalking in Tasmania. (Supplied: Urshla Connor)

While it can sometimes be difficult to get phone coverage in remote areas, bushwalkers should check for forecasts and warnings as often as possible on the bureau's website or the BOM Weather app.

"These days, it's easier than ever to check the forecast before you head out," Ms Connor said.

"I encourage everyone to read and understand the forecasts and warnings, and make sure they have the right clothing and equipment for the conditions.

World.title: Bulldogs junior runs out despite brother benched over gang war concerns
World.content:
Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs is allowing a promising young player in its ranks to continue playing despite his brother being benched over concerns for his safety due to familial links to Sydney's Alameddine crime family.

Bulldogs five-eighth Zain Alameddine ran out in the blue and white on Saturday in the Ron Massey Cup despite his brother, Parramatta Eels young gun Mohamed, being sidelined as a result of the city's escalating gang war.

The ABC can reveal the Bulldogs have been in extensive contact with the NRL Integrity Unit over Zain Alameddine's personal safety and ability to play.

The club has taken a series of measures to protect his safety, including providing security, who liaise directly with police at games he plays in.

The promising Bulldogs number seven only recently moved from Parramatta Eels himself. (Supplied)

The NRL's Integrity Unit has been working with NSW Police and providing advice to the Bulldogs on the matter, and has also done so for Parramatta.

The ABC understands that there is no immediate threat to Zain's safety and, as a result, Canterbury-Bankstown has opted to continue playing him, unlike Parramatta.

The Ron Massey Cup is the third-tier competition of semi-professional rugby league in New South Wales, while the NSW Cup is the highest level of competition and is one grade below the NRL, the professional competition.

Zain Alameddine has played predominantly in the Ron Massey Cup after playing earlier this year in the junior rugby league tournament, the SG Ball Cup.

Both Zain and Mohamed Alameddine are not accused of any wrongdoing, any involvement in organised crime, or the crime family bearing their last name.

Mohamed Alameddine is a development player for the Parramatta Eels.

The Alameddines operate a crime network out of Sydney's western suburbs, but its senior figures remain in hiding in Lebanon after fleeing the country in 2023.

Police believe a series of shootings and arson attacks over the past six months are linked to its feud with the self-proclaimed "Coconut Cartel", which takes its name from a historic slur against Pasifika people.

The decisions by the Bulldogs and the Eels come after a series of attacks between the two gangs spilling into public life.

One involved a foiled plot to kill an alleged member of the Alameddines at a suburban rugby league match in April.

The intended target, Ali Younes, was watching a game at Ringrose Park next to the Wenty Leagues Club when his alleged would-be assassins were spotted nearby and fled.

The ABC understands he was watching another Alameddine family member play.

Police intercepted that car and arrested three men at Homebush after pinning it along the M4 motorway, seizing a long-arm rifle and a pistol.

Three men were arrested and firearms seized after a car fled a suburban footy ground in April. (ABC News)

Police said during their pursuit of the car the three men inside allegedly threw jerry cans and bleach out of the window.

The car, police said, had been linked to a number of shootings before the Wentworthville plot.

Another incident in June saw a relative of the Alameddines and a young girl escape unharmed after a hitman's gun jammed in an attempted gangland assassination during a school pick-up in Fairfield.

New South Wales Rugby League has also been monitoring the situation and is in regular communication with both clubs; ultimately, decisions on who to select for the club remain with the club in both instances.

Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs did not respond to requests for comment, including why they have taken a different decision to Parramatta.

The ABC understands the club has worked closely to ensure Zain Alameddine can play safely and pursue his sporting dream.

The NRL, Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs and the NSWRL have all been contacted for comment.

World.title: Australia divided over how to tackle illegal tobacco crisis
World.content:
When the Australian Bureau of Statistics released data on tobacco consumption earlier this year it made headlines.

It found that 80 per cent of the tobacco consumed in Australia came from illicit sources.

It's a big number and highlights a deep problem for public health authorities and law enforcement alike.

Let's take a look at how we got there.

First, let's track the amount of legal tobacco consumed.

This chart using ABS figures shows the amount of nicotine consumed from legitimate cigarettes and tobacco, going back to 2016.

You can see the amounts don't really change much for the first few years, hovering around 4,500kg of nicotine per quarter.

This is despite yearly tax hikes, which would eventually make Australian cigarettes the most expensive in the world.

Then, halfway through 2019, the amount of legal tobacco starts to shift downwards.

... the tax hikes continue ...

… and the shift becomes a tumble.

Until we reach the latest numbers — about a third of where we were a decade ago.

A triumph for anti-tobacco campaigners and a big win for public health, right? Big tobacco on the run.

But this is not the whole chart. When people consume nicotine, the by-product is eventually flushed down the toilet, at which point a different story emerges.

This is the total nicotine detected in our wastewater...

Look at the gap between the lawful tobacco consumption and the story our wastewater is telling.

It is a huge rise in illegal nicotine consumption, and it's big headache for law enforcement.

This part shows the thousands of kilos of illicit cigarettes being smoked, according to ABS estimates.

Compare this with the amount of tobacco being consumed in illegal vapes. It's a much smaller but growing amount, which we'll go into...

This final section shows other nicotine products, like pouches, prescription nicotine and nicotine gum.

This all points to the black market trade fast becoming a replacement for Big Tobacco. And that brings problems of its own.

You'd be forgiven for thinking those figures mean eight out of every 10 cigarettes sold in Australia are illegal, and that smoking rates must be up.

That's what we first thought when we saw it. But it's not as simple as that (although the truth is not that far off).

Remember, the chart showed the volume of converted nicotine in wastewater, not the number of cigarettes being consumed, and that's an important difference.

Professor of Public Health at the University of Sydney, Becky Freeman, says the 80 per cent figure from the wastewater is most likely down to individuals consuming larger amounts of nicotine in illegal products.

Not only are the illegal cigarettes of varying strength, but it's likely that people who buy them are heavier users.

"What this suggests is that the people who are smoking illicit tobacco, are probably smoking more because there's no price barrier there."

Prof Freeman has worked in tobacco control for more than two decades and explains that all these figures are part of the same story.

"I'll just say none of these research findings are surprising to me," she says.

"They all marry up and paint a full picture."

The good news in all of that, she says, is that it doesn't mean smoking is back, as overall rates are down.

In a survey released last month, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare found daily smoking rates dropped to 5.6 per cent in 2025, down from 8.3 per cent in 2022 - 2023.

Although some, including Australia's former deputy chief medical officer Dr Nick Coatsworth, who supports a drop in excise, have questioned this figure, saying it goes against trends in several states, such as Western Australia, showing a lift in rates.

Authorities are cracking down on illicit tobacco sellers. ( )

Arson attacks and extortion are being used to control the illegal cigarette market. ( )

Nevertheless, that chart represents another problem — a huge hole in tax revenue.

Every dollar that goes to the black market is a dollar that's not going to taxpayers. Australia's Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner office estimates excise and duty evasion cost Australia up to $11.8 billion in the 2024-25 financial year.

In the latest federal budget, $8 billion was wiped off tobacco excise estimates over the next five years.

Smoking is still the leading cause of preventable death and disability in Australia and that comes with large price tag.

It's estimated smoking costs the economy more than $136 billion a year in the treatment of diseases (including heart disease and lung and oesophageal cancers) as well as lost productivity.

Low risk, high reward for criminals

So, now we can see how we got here, how can we solve the problem?

Not everyone agrees to the same approach. Dr James Martin says Australia is seeing a "mass consumer revolt" against the price of cigarettes.

The Deakin University criminologist points out that a pack-a-day smoker would be looking at a bill of more than $15,000.

"I'm surprised that the government has continued to double down on the policies that have gotten us here rather than looking for alternative approaches," he says.

"So you take an addictive commodity, you price it out of a range of affordability, there's very little difference between banning something outright ... or just pricing it out of availability.

"The net effect is the same, and that is that it displaces demand to illicit operators."

Perceived as a low-risk and high-reward business model, selling illicit tobacco has become one of the fastest growing criminal markets.

It's now second only to illicit drugs in lining the pockets of organised crime groups.

So what are the solutions?

Shouldn't we cut tobacco tax?

Given the chart shows a clear increase in illicit tobacco consumption as the price of legal products steadily rises, it seems like the first place to start.

But this is where ideas on how to tackle the issue differ most. The federal government is cold on any change to the tobacco tax.

Assistant Minister for Customs Julian Hill told the ABC in June that reducing the excise "doesn't stand up to scrutiny".

"What magic level of excise reduction would make any material difference to transnational and serious organise crime profitability?" he said.

"The option is not to surrender our nation's health policy to organised crime or condemn the next generation to the scourge of smoking-related disease and early death."

On the other side of politics, Liberal MP Mary Aldred says the excise is "too high" and a reduction should be considered as part of a "Swiss army knife of solutions".

"The price point legal cigarettes are now at means the government is driving honest, decent Australians into the arms of organised crime," she said at a National Press Club address last month.

In Ms Aldred's hometown of Warragul, a suspected illegal tobacco shop was firebombed 80 metres from her electorate office, terrifying nearby businesses and the small community.

"There's thousands of small business owners right across Australia who have nothing to do with this and are losing trading hours, they're losing staff, because they are scared about coming to work and no-one's standing up for them," she told the Press Club.

"I believe this will come to be seen as the greatest public policy failing in a generation."

NSW Premier Chris Minns has also called on the federal government to consider lowering the tobacco excise, questioning whether it is the best use of NSW Police time to be fighting on the illegal tobacco front.

Professor Richard Holden from the UNSW Business School believes it is a "huge mistake" for the government not to consider changing the excise.

The economist is calling for the excise to be cut entirely for a period of time, while authorities get on top of the black market.

"It's a disaster ... because if you make the excise high enough, you create an incentive for illicit tobacco to come into the country," he says.

Emergency services on the scene of a tobacco store fire in Melbourne's south-east in 2025. ( )

Thousands of tonnes of tobacco have been found by authorities. ( )

Border force officers have uncovered hundreds of tonnes of illegal tobacco. ( )

But Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner Amber Shuhyta is not advocating for excise cut. "It is not my current understanding that reducing the excise rate would effectively shift the market dynamic," she says.

She says she doesn't want to have "blinkers on" looking at one policy lever.

The commissioner says the market is currently being driven by not only the price differences, but also the sophistication of organised crime networks, the technologies that became available to them in recent years, the rise in the number of shops selling the illegal products, and the demand for what is a highly addictive commodity.

Professor Freeman wants to see more control on the market, not less.

"I don't think people realise that illicit tobacco can get even cheaper. It's not being sold at the most basement bargain price already. It's really cheap to manufacture cigarettes," Professor Freeman says.

"So all we would be doing (in cutting the tax) is trying to 'compete' with criminal gangs."

The Australian Medical Association also says reducing tobacco excise would increase prevalence and "undo decades of effective public health strategy".

Ok, well how about tougher policing?

Last year Australian Border Force seized more than 2.66 billion illegal cigarettes, up from 480 million in 2016.

The products mostly come in two forms. Counterfeit cigarettes that look and taste like legitimate brands, but are not made by the company advertised on the branding.

The other is cigarettes made legally in another country, but smuggled and sold in Australia without duties or taxes.

With vapes only legally sold at pharmacies, almost every vape bought in Australia is unlawful — 97 per cent of e-cigarettes sold are from illegal sources, which amounts to a market value of $1.6 billion.

The federal government has committed $84 million over the last two budgets for enforcement, storage and disposal.

It's part of a $345 million strategy to try and disrupt the illegal market, which includes the National Disruption Group, an ABF-led team that works with state and territory police.

The Australian Border Force seize illicit cigarettes imported through international mail. ( )

The Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission says organised crime groups involved in the illegal trade show "the agility and sophistication of multinational businesses".

"Without sustained and coordinated intervention, the market will continue to expand and further entrench criminal influence in Australia," it said in its submission to a Liberal-led senate inquiry into illegal tobacco due to report on August 13.

But Dr James Martin says arresting big players can also have the opposite effect, and entrench black markets further.

"Policing doesn't work against illicit markets that big," he says.

"And that's because the distribution networks are dense and there's so many players in the market that if you take one out ... not just one retailer, but a whole syndicate, there are so many other competitors in the space."

If policing won't work, how about new penalties?

Commissioner Shuhyta is firm that Australia needs to harden the environment for anyone trying to sell illegal tobacco.

"It is about strengthening consequences," she says.

"It's about centralising all of our data and intelligence and information, so we can tackle this in a national way rather than separate agencies going alone."

Tobacco licensing is state or territory based, so a range of laws are in place across the country.

Australian Border Force has seized tonnes of illgal tobacco. ( )

The Australian Border Force disrupte a major illicit tobacco operation in the Northern Territory. ( )

The Police Association has called for a nationally consistent licensing scheme for the sale of tobacco.

Two years ago, Victoria promised some of the toughest penalties in the country after dozens of arson attacks linked to the so-called tobacco wars.

New penalties mean anyone caught with illegal tobacco faces fines of up to $370,000 or 15 years' jail and businesses face penalties of more than $1.8 million.

One Victoria Police detective told the ABC's 7.30 that after 500 arrests he wasn't sure law enforcement was making a dent.

"They [organised crime groups] have got bigger budgets than law enforcement agencies, which is just frightening."

There's also been crackdowns in WA, with 50 shops in Perth shut down by authorities last month. Queensland Health has issued 275 shop closure orders since November last year and NSW tightened its licensing scheme and increased fines.

Can we cut smoking rates further?

There is wide agreement that it's best to have as few smokers as possible.

Smoke-free products such as vapes, gums and pouches have been touted by the tobacco industry as a lesser evil than inhaling the toxic fumes of cigarettes.

But the products remain highly controversial, with health groups concerned they simply shift the nicotine addiction to another product.

Last month the government cracked down on nicotine pouches, closing a loophole for personal importation, in a bid to reduce their availability.

"Anyone unlawfully selling nicotine pouches in Australia has been put on notice," Minister for Health Mark Butler said.

Dr Coatsworth says there needs to be a shift to talking about harm reduction but admits it is a "wicked public policy problem".

"We must either temporarily align with some of the objectives of the worst corporate citizens on the planet, or surrender our youth or disadvantaged smokers to an illegal market," he told the Press Club.

He says alternatives such as vapes and tobacco pouches should be considered to get long-term smokers to kick the habit.

Professor Freeman is more cautious.

"The only way I would be comfortable with these products being available for Australians to use is if they had that stamp of approval that they were safe and effective for smoking cessation. And no company has."

Dr Martin says Sweden has been able to drive down its smoking rates to under 5 per cent of the population with the availability of non-combustible nicotine options, such as tobacco pouches and a product developed in the country called snus, which is absorbed into a person's lip.

Illegal cigarettes don't contain health warnings like legal products. ( )

But others fear that opening the door to alternatives is inviting Big Tobacco in the back door.

There were deep concerns that the senate inquiry allowed tobacco giant Philip Morris a closed-door hearing, with a coalition of health organisations calling it out in an open letter.

"The only way I would be comfortable with these products being available for Australians to use is if they had that stamp of approval that they were safe and effective for smoking cessation. And no company has," Professor Freeman says.

"We need to do more in tobacco control, not less.

"What we're doing is working. We need to hold the course."

She wants to see cigarettes harder to come by in Australia.

"They should only be sold in a few places that can handle the intense responsibility of selling such a dangerous, addictive and highly taxed product."

Commissioner Shuhyta says a coordinated response is needed.

"I don't just listen to the loudest voices," she says.

"I think diversity in thinking is a good thing. I think we need to contest ideas. I think we need to have all of the different perspectives at the table because just looking at it through one lens will not get us the solution we need."

About the reporting

The ABS chart of household consumption of illicit tobacco and nicotine products uses experimental estimates of illicit tobacco consumption, using quarterly wastewater data sourced from the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission.

Samples were collected from 60 wastewater treatment plants cross Australia, representing about 60 per cent of Australia’s total population.

While wastewater data provides reliable estimates of total nicotine consumption, it does not identify which products the nicotine came from. Information from existing survey and administrative data sources, such as supermarket scanner data and ATO tax data, is used to establish nicotine consumption from legal tobacco products. The Kalman filter approach is used to allocate the remaining unobserved nicotine consumption across all product types and quantities.

Credits

World.title: Tupac was a 'global megastar', then his murder created an enduring mystery
World.content:
Before he became one of the most influential rappers of all time, before the movies and the albums that would catapult him to global fame, before he found himself at the centre of a bloody East-West Coast hip-hop rivalry, Tupac Shakur was drama kid at a high school in Baltimore.

Richard Pilcher, the school's principal acting instructor at the time, remembers a "charismatic" and "polite" young boy.

"I know that that seems counterintuitive with the whole thug persona," he told the ABC.

"You could see that he had a lot of talent, and a ton of charisma, a killer smile, and amazing eyes.

Tupac Shakur in the 1988 Baltimore School for the Arts yearbook.

"Did I foresee that he was going to be a global megastar? No, I thought he might've had a career, if he got the breaks, but I couldn't foresee that."

Shakur's promising career was cut short when he was just 25, in a Las Vegas drive-by shooting that would fuel countless conspiracy theories and a 30-year murder mystery

The case went cold for years, until a member of a rival gang released a tell-all memoir in which he said he was involved in Shakur's death.

Now, for the first time, the circumstances surrounding the rapper's murder will be prosecuted in court.

And after three decades, the world may get some answers about who killed the young superstar — and why.

The birth of a megastar

Tupac Shakur was born in 1971 in East Harlem, New York, and named after an indigenous Peruvian revolutionary.

His mother Afeni Shakur — freshly out of jail when she gave birth to him — had been active in the Black Panther Party and wanted her son to carry the name of a powerful man of colour.

Shakur's godmother Assata Shakur was also a Black Panther and an infamous member of the Black Liberation Army who was found guilty of killing a New Jersey state trooper but maintained her innocence and escaped from prison, fleeing to Cuba.

Both women would shape his understanding of race, oppression and justice, themes that would permeate his music in years to come.

Shakur in a scene from the film Gridlock'd, released in 1997. (Photo by Gramercy Pictures/Getty Images)

At 13, Shakur moved with his family to Baltimore where he studied acting, poetry, jazz and ballet at the Baltimore School for the Arts.

It's there he first met Mr Pilcher.

"We had a particular connection, I think, because I taught Shakespeare and he loved Shakespeare, which is not a surprise," he said.

"He loved words, he loved language."

One of Shakur's poems was featured amongst his notebooks in the Tupac Shakur - Wake Me When I'm Free exhibition in Los Angeles, 2022. (AP Photo: Chris Pizzello)

The young thespian thrived at the school and developed a lifelong friendship with fellow student Jada Pinkett who also became an actor after graduating.

But in 1988, Shakur and his family left Baltimore and headed west to California, seeking an escape from the poverty, housing instability and drug addiction that had plagued his mother in the east.

Mr Pilcher said the teenager was "crushed" by the move.

"He had really found a home, I think, where he was respected and valued, had friends and mentors, and he was really upset that he had to leave that."

West Coast — where he found fame… and trouble

It was on the West Coast where Tupac Shakur became immersed in hip-hop culture and his career accelerated.

In a few short years, he went from being a dancer and backup rapper to one of hip-hop's biggest stars.

He released four studio albums, including All Eyez on Me, the first double-disc studio album in hip-hop history, which would go on to become one of the best-selling rap albums of all time.

He also starred in seven feature films, including opposite Janet Jackson in Poetic Justice.

Shakur (left) with founder of Death Row Records Marion "Suge" Knight (right). (AP Photo: Frank Wiese, File)

But it was also on the West Coast where he found himself embroiled in a fierce rivalry between opposing music scenes and record labels.

The East Coast-West Coast feud centred on Death Row Records in Los Angeles and Bad Boy Records in New York.

Marion "Suge" Knight was the co-founder of Death Row records alongside producer Dr Dre, with acts like Snoop Dogg signed to the label.

On the East Coast, Sean "Diddy" Combs founded Bad Boy Records which included rappers like The Notorious B.I.G.

The record labels' feud spilled beyond the music industry, and into violence.

Death Row Records hired security guards associated with part of the Bloods gang, which was founded in Los Angeles to compete against another group, the Crips.

A part of that group, the South Side Compton Crips, had close ties with Bad Boy Records.

Tupac Shakur seen arriving at court on sexual assault charges after a shooting in 1994. (AP Photo: Eric Miller, File)

The growing rift between the two factions spilled into violence in 1994, when Shakur was shot five times during an apparent robbery at a New York recording studio.

He survived the incident but it inflamed tensions between the two sides.

The murder, the investigation, the conspiracies

The East-West feud hit its peak on September 7, 1996.

After attending a Mike Tyson fight in Nevada, Shakur and Knight got in a car to make their way to a nearby nightclub where Shakur was due to perform.

As they drove along the glitzy Las Vegas Strip, dotted with its casinos, flashing lights and tourists, a white Cadillac pulled up alongside them.

Tupac Shakur and Marion "Suge" Knight, in a photo snapped just minutes before the shooting. (Supplied: Wikimedia Commons/Leonard Jefferson)

A passenger in the back seat then rolled down their window and opened fire.

Shakur was shot four times while Knight was grazed by a bullet.

Cathy Scott, who was a crime reporter for the Las Vegas Sun at the time, remembers the night well.

"I was asleep and I got the telephone call from a homicide detective who said 'get down to the Las Vegas strip right now, a rapper by the name of Tupac Shakur has been shot'," she told the ABC.

The black BMW Shakur was killed in, riddled with bullet holes, in a Las Vegas police impound lot in 1996. (AP Photo: Lennox McLendon, File)

Shakur was admitted to hospital, but died six days later.

From the beginning, Scott says the police handled the case with a level of secrecy she had never experienced. She says someone within the police department told her it was because they were worried about bad publicity.

"Rappers, thugs and that sort of thing they thought would be bad for tourism," she said.

"That was always the bottom dollar, it still is."

And in the absence of official information, an industry of conspiracy theories grew and festered.

Some speculated, without evidence, that it was an inside job by one of Shakur's own crew. Others guessed the shooting was linked to his mother's Black Panther legacy.

There were even people who claimed Shakur had faked his own death.

The intersection of Harmon and Las Vegas Boulevard, where Shakur was shot the day before. (AP Photo: Jack Dempsey, File)

"Because the police didn't respond immediately, I think that … helped fuel the conspiracies and all the ridiculousness behind it," said Scott, who wrote a book about Shakur's killing.

The shooting sparked a "bloodbath" of retaliatory violence in Compton, Scott said. But eventually the East-West rivalry faded and the case went cold.

Years passed, witnesses died holding onto their secrets and it seemed no-one would ever be held accountable for the killing of Shakur.

That is, until Duane "Keffe D" Davis, a self-identified leader in the South Side Compton Crips, began talking about the case.

A tell-all memoir leads to first murder charge

In 2019, Davis released a tell-all memoir — Compton Street Legend — in which he admitted to being involved in Tupac Shakur's shooting.

Duane Davis arrives for a motion hearing in August for his upcoming trial on murder charges in the 1996 killing of Shakur. (Reuters: Ethan Miller)

In it, Davis says he was sitting in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed a gun into the back seat.

The memoir says Shakur and his entourage had "crossed the line" by beating up Davis's nephew Orlando Anderson hours before the shooting.

"We couldn't let no record company studio gangsters do us like that," it reads.

Davis's book does not name who pulled the trigger. Three other people were in the car at the time, but they have all since died. None of them faced charges.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis' memoir Compton Street Legend will be front and centre of his trial. (Reuters: Ethan Miller)

In his memoir, Davis described himself — and Knight, who has also since written a memoir — as the "only living eyewitnesses to what truly happened".

In September 2023, Duane Davis was charged with orchestrating the killing of Tupac Shakur.

He has pleaded not guilty.

'Bigger in death than he was in life'

Thirty years later, Scott still sees Shakur's death as an overwhelming tragedy.

"The whole saga … it's just so sad, from beginning to end," she said.

In the three decades since that night, Shakur's legend and legacy has only grown and Scott says he's now "bigger in death than he was in life".

People take pictures of Shakur's star during its posthumous unveiling ceremony on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2023. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

His posthumously-released track Changes became a major protest anthem in the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, vaulting it back into the music charts and reigniting conversations about racism, police brutality and inequality that had been central themes for Shakur.

He'd gone from reading poetry under a streetlight because the electricity was disconnected at home to a global superstar at just 25.

T.I., YG and Snoop Dogg perform a tribute to Shakur at his 2017 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony. (AP: Charles Sykes)

Scott believes, given a chance, he would have become even bigger.

"He was so smart and … I think he would've become a spokesperson for his era," Scott said.

"He could have been a congressman for all we know … he had a big, big future and he was so bright."

Davis's trial is set to begin in Las Vegas on Monday, local time.

World.title: High interest rates here to stay, but only one part of house price story
World.content:
We seem to have flipped from worrying about rising house prices to worrying about falling house prices.

Well, some of us have, anyway.

Last Tuesday's front-page lead in The Australian, reporting the July house price data, was "$230 billion hit: value going, going, gone", describing it as a "once-in-a-generation housing slump".

It does sound like a lot, but it is just a 1.8 per cent decline from $12.77 trillion to $12.54 trillion, so just an old-fashioned page-one beat-up.

Next day, they followed up with "ALP turns blind eye to house market mugging", another beat-up, quoting NAB's new forecast that house prices in major east coast cities (Melbourne and Sydney) will fall 10 per cent.

But since the low point of February 2023, the national median house price has increased another 35 per cent, a compound annual growth of more than 10 per cent and a fabulous, unexpected windfall to home owners as well as a devastating lockout for those who are not.

That happened even after interest rates increased four more times in 2023 and then stayed there, followed by three cuts last year and three hikes this year.

That was caused by a blowout in immigration in 2022-23, a massive increase in construction costs after the pandemic and a decline in dwelling approvals.

If house prices did fall 10 per cent from this year's peak, it would indeed be a "once-in-a-generation" event since the largest decline in the past 50 years was 8 per cent in both 2010 and 2017.

It would reduce the rise since February 2023 back to 20 per cent and result in a slight improvement in Australia's very poor housing affordability.

Will it happen?

Possibly, but it's complicated, and impossible to predict.

Loading...

End of the low interest rate era

The two reasons prices are falling now are this year's three rate hikes and the budget changes to negative gearing and capital gains taxation, causing some investors to get out, as intended.

Against that, Treasury predicted that those budget changes would eventually result in fewer houses being built, so it's possible that the longer-term impact of them will be higher prices.

Have interest rates already peaked? With two Australian banks cutting fixed home loan rates, there is a ray of hope that the cycle of interest rate hikes has peaked and borrowing costs may be lower down the track — another sign the pace of economic change has moved into overdrive.

As for interest rates, the Reserve Bank is certain to leave them on hold when it meets today and tomorrow and very likely to keep them there for the rest of the year, although the futures market is putting a 64 per cent chance on a hike in 2026 … along with a 63 per cent chance of a cut in 2027, as the economy slows in response to the cuts.

In general, though, the days of super-low interest rates that characterised the decade from 2012 to 2022, and which pushed house prices up by 60 per cent, are over — unless there is another GFC or pandemic (which can't be ruled out, of course, with share prices at record highs and bird flu on the march).

Bond markets have taken the 10-year interest rate to 5 per cent — the highest in 15 years — as part of a global rise in government bond yields.

That is happening because a surge in spending on data centres and defence has collided with historically high government debt.

That collision has brought decades of savings glut to an end and is likely to lead to structurally higher interest rates for decades to come.

Enter AI

Political populism has permanently increased government spending and lowered taxation, while the end of globalisation and America's role as the guarantor of peace has meant that all countries must now spend more on defence.

Meanwhile, the arrival of AI has dramatically increased the need for more "compute", or computer processing capacity, produced in factories known as data centres.

The amount of computing used in an AI query is potentially 10 times higher than the now-redundant Google search, partly because it usually results in a dialogue rather than simply a list of links, but also because you can do far more with AI, such as create videos and photos and write software code.

On top of that, the number of queries is multiplying exponentially because of the Jevons paradox, which states that as efficiency lowers the effective cost of using a resource, demand grows and often outpaces the initial savings.

The effect of those two multiplications is that the demand for compute is increasing about 3,000 to 5,000-fold, resulting in a huge increase in the number of data centres.

Whether there will be enough money made from AI to service the colossal amount of capital raised to build them, especially now that China has spoiled the US oligopoly party, is another matter, and is causing some anxiety among investors (but not most of them — share prices are at record highs, so optimism still rules).

And this is before the next phase of AI takes hold — that is, humanoid robots, also described as "physical AI".

My X (Twitter) feed at the moment is full of videos of robots expertly doing all sorts of jobs, like mopping the floor, making hotel beds, building a house, laying bricks, kneading bread dough, making furniture, and picking tomatoes.

I'd say most, if not all, of these are fake — AI videos based on humans doing the work and made to look like robots — but I can't be sure. And anyway, it's early days. It won't be long before robots can do all those things, and more.

This is not the place for a philosophical discussion about what this means, and how bakers, hotel staff, bricklayers, carpenters and fruit-pickers will be occupied and paid, but it obviously means a lot — for the future of work and humanity itself, as well as the demand for compute and data centres.

Bottom line: high interest rates are here to stay, which will continue to weigh on house prices.

But that is only part of the housing story; physical demand and supply are important as well, which is where the complications come in.

Loading

The role of migration

The Labor government seems to be in the process of turning Treasury's migration forecast in the budget into a target, as a part of its defence against One Nation as well as the housing affordability project.

The forecast for 2025-26 was increased from 260,000 to 295,000 in the nick of time; it's likely to have been exceeded but not by much — only by 10,000 or so.

ABC Business Daily podcast The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy.

The forecast of 225,000 for the current financial year and beyond will be a more challenging target because a lot of it is demand-driven and not even identified by the government, let alone controlled, as we learned in 2022-23 when Treasury forecast net overseas migration of 180,000 and it turned out to be 513,000.

If they plan to get net overseas migration down from 300,000 or so to 225,000 this year by using the lever they do control, which is skilled migration, that could be a problem, since one of the reasons for a shortage of housing is a shortage of tradies, which the industry is desperately urging the government to address with more skilled migration.

You could do it by having fewer business undergraduates and cooks and more construction workers, but that would require a level of intervention the government has so far either avoided or failed to achieve.

(In the years following World War II, the Labor government did intervene, setting up offices around the UK and Europe to recruit tradespeople and paying for them to get here, so it's not impossible.)

The other target — of building 1.2 million homes over five years from 2024 under the National Housing Accord — is already proving a challenge, or rather "ambitious", as the government prefers to call it.

States and local councils can release all the land they want, and increase height limits around stations, but if there aren't enough people to build them, and enough developers prepared to take the risk, the houses and apartments won't get built.

Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That’s Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

World.title: Israeli government rejects Trump's Gaza peace plan
World.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has expressly rejected the latest Trump administration-backed push for peace in Gaza, criticising Hamas's proposed process for disarming as "unacceptable".

Speaking ahead of his weekly Sunday cabinet meeting, Mr Netanyahu said his government was in discussions with the United States on the matter and acknowledged the two countries had differing views.

"They have ideas, some of them are acceptable to us and some are unacceptable to us," he said.

"Israel rejects the 15-point plan.

Thousands of Palestinians remain displaced within Gaza, months after a ceasefire came into force. (Reuters: Dawoud Abu Alkas)

"The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until the dismantling of Hamas and its weapons — and when I say dismantling Hamas and its weapons, that means heavy weaponry, less heavy weaponry and smaller arms, all weaponry.

"We're talking about a true dismantling, not a fictitious dismantling."

Palestinians doubt Hamas weapons deal will hold Palestinians in Gaza have expressed scepticism about Hamas's declaration it will lay down its weapons in a bid to kickstart the stalled peace process, concerned it will not actually change the situation in the war-ravaged strip.

Just over a week ago, US President Donald Trump was heralding a major breakthrough in the peace process after his Board of Peace brokered a deal for Hamas to hand over its weapons.

Hours after making his announcement on social media, he claimed Israel was "very happy about it", comments now at odds with Mr Netanyahu's remarks.

The Israeli prime minister's rhetoric is not entirely surprising, given much of the Israeli establishment has railed against the proposal for the past week.

But it does show how difficult negotiations on reaching the next phase of the ceasefire in Gaza will be, particularly ahead of an Israeli election, and proves that there are some limits to the White House's sway over the Netanyahu government.

Since October 2025, when the truce was announced, Palestinian health authorities reported more than 1,200 people had been killed in Israeli strikes, among them many women and children.

Israel intensifies strikes on Gaza

In announcing it would disarm on Friday, July 31, Hamas revealed there were certain conditions which needed to be met by Israel.

Specifically, Israel would need to stop almost daily deadly attacks across the strip and its forces would need to withdraw from large swathes of territory.

Since the ceasefire in Gaza was declared, Israel has pushed deeper into the strip — increasing its control from just over 50 per cent of the land to over 60 per cent.

The Yellow Line, the name given to the boundary of Israeli control, has moved during that period, displacing more Palestinians in the process.

Hamas also said it would hand over its weapons for storage by the new US-backed Palestinian technocratic organisation, known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.

It still has not been allowed to enter the strip by Israel, and has been forced to conduct its affairs from the Egyptian capital Cairo.

Israel is refusing to withdraw its forces from occupied parts of the strip. (Reuters: Amir Cohen)

Hours after Hamas's declaration, Israel unleashed some of its deadliest attacks on the strip, prompting a thinly veiled rebuke from the Trump administration's Board of Peace, and its High Representative for Gaza Nickolay Mladenov.

Mr Mladenov met with Mr Netanyahu in Israel days later. The Reuters news agency is reporting Israel agreed to show restraint in some of its strikes.

"We expect the mediators and the US guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons, while continuing to jeopardise the region's security and stability," Hamas official Basem Naim told Reuters.

The Israeli prime minister also, once again, rejected any notion of potential Palestinian statehood, which is a politically sensitive issue in Israel at any moment, let alone before an election.

"As long as I am prime minister, a Palestinian state will not be established," he said.

"Not in Gaza and not in Judea and Samaria, not a 'Fatah-stan' and not a 'Hamas-stan'."

Judea and Samaria is the Biblical name for the area commonly referred to as the West Bank.

World.title: Albanese is the opposite of Rudd and that comes with its own risks
World.content:
It's a tale of two prime ministers.

When Kevin Rudd was prime minister, the standing joke among colleagues was that they would line up and rush to get their work ticked off whenever his deputy, Julia Gillard, was acting PM.

It was one of the early signals that despite a landslide election victory, Rudd's autocratic style and habit of labouring over decisions was eroding his authority.

This week a senior government source told me the opposite was now the case.

Ministers instead look to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese whenever there is a contentious or difficult decision to be made.

That was on full display last week, with the cabinet unable to land a position on Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke's proposal on immigration cuts.

Instead, members of cabinet decided to defer a decision until the PM was back on deck, a measure of Albanese's dominance.

The leak of the cabinet stalemate over immigration policy was a rare lapse in discipline for the government. That it happened while Albanese was away shows how firm his grip on the party is, even if some of his colleagues are already thinking about becoming his successor.

The policy dispute has already been framed by some as a left-right brawl. But in reality, it's about the budget, stupid.

Migration and economy linked

Cuts to migration and tighter visa rules have a material impact on the budget bottom line. Fewer people in Australia potentially means fewer taxpayers than forecast.

In the feverish debate about immigration, the economic cost is often ignored, yet that part of Burke's proposal proved most contentious among some ministers.

Burke delays speech The ABC understands the cuts to migration numbers are contentious within Labor, but no reason for the delay is given.

Asked this week about the impact of migration cuts on business, Pauline Hanson said she did not care.

"I don't care what people think. Whether it's going to affect their businesses [because] they're not going to sell that many products," Hanson said on Thursday.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce said such a move would deter skilled migrants from coming to Australia, undermine the migration system and hurt the economy.

Labor doesn't have the luxury of not caring what business thinks or what impact immigration cuts may have on the economy.

The ALP has gone to great effort to put the issue of migration back in a box, including keeping the Liberal government's policy architecture of offshore detention and boat turnbacks, much to the discomfort of many rank-and-file members, as well as some in caucus.

That last week's cabinet debate was over that issue and the fact the policy remains seemingly unresolved proves a messy and unwelcome return to Labor being under scrutiny on immigration.

Two alternatives line up

Parliament resumes on Tuesday and the tale of two prime ministers will become a tale of two alternative leaders: Angus Taylor and Pauline Hanson.

Taylor might be the official opposition leader, but Hanson is the de facto.

Political analysis that matters The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

For Taylor, this week will be a test of whether he can take paint off the government.

Hanson's job will be easier: any day migration is the main story she can deploy her skill of tying the issue to housing and broader cost-of-living pressures.

For Albanese, the ministers who rely on him to make the call on key cabinet decisions will be again looking to him to clean up last week's mess.

Migration is no longer a social policy argument. It is now seen through the prism of being about roads, rents and the cost of living. This has given Hanson and One Nation room to be an alternative voice to government.

Albanese will have to show Labor understands those pressures while ensuring the government's policy doesn't risk the ire of parts of multicultural communities.

The PM will also want to avoid looking like this isn't a response to Hanson.

If Albanese can't get hold of this issue, he risks opening a flank the two leaders, Taylor and Hanson, will happily spend the parliament sitting week trying to make even wider.

Loading

Labor rolls dice on gambling bill

Then there is gambling. The PM will be trying to sort out the mess the government's long-awaited gambling legislation is becoming.

The most direct path to pass the legislation needs the support of either the Greens or Coalition and as it stands both want the reforms to go further.

Albanese's allies often evangelise his political instincts. He will need them to broker a deal to get the legislation passed and off the government's to-do list.

Gambling reform might not shift many votes, but it tells voters whether the government can stand up to corporate giants like the betting industry or continue to bend to their power.

It will again be Albanese that will make the call on what compromises the government is up for.

Being relied on to make the tough calls reinforces his authority, but it also leaves him carrying all the risk and, if things go wrong, all the blame.

Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

World.title: Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress
World.content:
An independent report that found just 54 of the government’s 270 promised mental health reforms had been completed was reworked ahead of its publication to credit it with doubling progress on royal commission recommendations. The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission’s original report also had its judging criteria changed, its ratings improved, and its most critical findings removed in the months after it was first presented to the government. The delayed release and reworking of the report has drawn criticism over the stalled overhaul of the sector following the royal commission and raised concerns that the government is undermining the independence of bodies meant to hold it to account. Even the original report’s author, former Commissioner Annabel Brebner, cast doubt over the credibility of the re-worked findings.



“The initial method emphasised transparency of reporting of progress in implementing the recommendations, and the categories used to assess progress reflected this,” she said in a short statement. “In my view, the difference in methodology raises questions about the overall reliability and validity of the assessments made.” Brebner added she had not contacted the MHWC or sought and explanation on why the report’s content had altered so dramatically. The commission’s long-awaited status update into Victoria’s mental health reforms was presented to the government in December 2025. However, it was not published until June 24, 2026, and, during the six-month delay, at least 75 of the independent commissioners’ original 270 status ratings were improved.



A leaked draft of the commissioners’ original report, which was sent to the Department of Health and some key stakeholders, reveals huge changes were made to the MHWC’s assessments to favour the government’s position. Many of the strongest concerns raised in the original draft – including the impact of budget cuts, a lack of evidence to support government claims and the refusal of stakeholders to work with the Department of Health – are also missing from the publicly released version in June. In one example, four of the five sub-recommendations relating to Aboriginal social and emotional wellbeing reforms have been upgraded from “partial progress” in December, to “in place” in July, while the sentence “the 2025-26 Budget did not include funding for further development of these initiatives” was cut from its findings. By the time the report was released the commissioners who wrote the original version had been removed from their positions by an act of parliament, and an interim commissioner, appointed directly by Minister for Mental Health Ingrid Stitt, had overseen its redrafting and public release.



Three senior mental health figures familiar with the report’s delay refused to discuss the circumstances of its rewriting on the record, fearing reprisals from the government and further financial cuts to vital services. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Mental health watchdog muzzled by ‘drastic’ budget cuts “We have essentially lost independent oversight of the royal commission,” one source said. Another accused the government of undermining the commission’s ability to monitor the failing sector, including slashing its 2025-26 budget to 40 per cent below its forecast expenses, cutting its staff from 54 to 27, and hobbling its independence. “The royal commission’s findings were not just about new services, but about improved system governance, outcomes, and culture,” they said.



“To have such a governance body be defunded and demoted before an election, and information withheld by bureaucrats until the minister’s appointee is in control, shows that not much has actually changed on that front, if not getting worse.” It follows revelations in July that a 33-page CFA report, which gave a blunt assessment of the shortcomings in the state’s firefighting capability, was whitewashed after talks with the state government and cut back to 18 pages. An Instagram post from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission on April 28, 2026 - the day an act of parliament eliminated the role of the commissioners, and the day the Department of Health provided new information to allow for the redrafting of their independent evaluation of the government’s mental health system overhauls. The MHWC was established in 2022 to independently monitor and report annually on the Victorian government’s progress of implementing the mental health royal commission’s recommendations. It was headed by four commissioners, including two with lived experience. Work on its latest report was led by Brebner during 2025 before being reviewed by the watchdog’s full team of commissioners and the CEO.



The commission briefed the Department of Health about its findings in November 2025, and asked for a government response so it could be included in the document before its potential publication in December or January. Two sources familiar with those discussions said Brebner and her team grew frustrated at the government’s refusal to provide a response,and agitated to release the report without one, but were blocked by the then commission chair Maggie Toko. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health ‘Serious step backwards’: Furious response from mental health sector to cost-cutting bill On December 4, 2025, the government introduced to parliament a controversial bill to overhaul the commission’s leadership and limit it’s investigative remit - in contravention of the royal commission’s recommendation - paving the way to replace the four independent commissioners with a single commissioner. A fortnight later, on December 16, the MHWC report was sent to staff and key stakeholders to brief them ahead of an possible January release, which was then repeatedly delayed.



Brebner, fellow commissioners and MHWC staff continued to push for the report’s release up to April 27, when the legislative changes came into effect and their positions were eliminated. Toko was appointed interim Mental Health and Wellbeing Commissioner by Stitt. Footnotes in the published report show that just one day later the Department of Health provided the MHWC with a raft of “authorised information”, allowing for the document’s redrafting. Some of those familiar the original MHWC’s original independent assessments said they were shocked at the extent of changes when the implementation status update was finally released on June 24. A comparison of the documents shows while the original report assigned five possible status ratings for progress on each of the royal commission’s 270 sub-recommendations, the published report cut that to just three.



That included the removal of a category titled “limited evidence of progress available publicly”, which had been assigned to 32 cases where no evidence of work being undertaken, other than press releases and other announcements, could be found. Another rating category, “to be assessed later”, was also deleted. It had been given to 26 sub-recommendations in the original report, where the commissioners deemed new programs were too fresh to be assessed in a meaningful way. The changes left three wider ratings remaining - Not Yet Commenced; Partial Progress; and In Place - and saw at least 75 grades from the original report improved in the one published June. Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said the commission had been established to hold government and service providers to account. “The claims that the government re-wrote and delayed a critical report assessing the government’s performance on mental health is a blow for transparency and accountability,” he said.



“Under the legislation the commission is meant to act as an independent body. This means being free from government interference.” “Good government requires independent advice, scrutiny, and accountability. Yet the Labor government has long engaged in the politicisation of the public service, and independent bodies like the commission, which only weakens democracy.” When asked why its assessments changed, the MHWC told The Age that its December 2025 version was “an early, incomplete draft” that had “gaps or inaccuracies” because it had not been provided with departmental information, and was not approved for release at that stage. It said the report was updated when the department’s response was provided, and this information “informed, but did not determine” its findings.



“At the halfway point of the 10-year mental health reform agenda, the commission sought to highlight both – the progress to date in delivering on recommendations since the royal commission, as well as to highlight the important work still ahead, with detail, accuracy and balance,” Interim Commissioner Maggie Toko said. ”It is important that the commission’s reporting provide the community and all stakeholders with an accurate and comprehensive view on the status of the implementation of the recommendations for mental health reform, that conveys the progress to date, and a sense of optimism and continued commitment towards the ongoing work in improving outcomes into the future.” The Department of Health said it had been provided with a draft of the MHWC’s report at the end of 2025, and provided “factual and technical feedback” between December 2025 and May 2026 to ensure it had up-to-date information. “The MHWC is an independent statutory authority – it is responsible for its own reports, findings and assessments, including decisions about content and publication dates,” a department spokesperson said.
