World.title: ‘I think you can do it all’: Can Robert Irwin make the Logies relevant again?
World.content:
What business does a 22-year-old, who belongs to a generation that barely engages with traditional media, have hosting the most traditional night on Australian TV?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A



“And so now, particularly after doing a lot more on free-to-air television in Australia, now all my mates were excited for the next season of I’m a Celeb or, ‘Oh, that’s so cool, you’re hosting the Logies’. So my job is to bring that next generation into what we’ve all grown up enjoying. Because I think young people probably don’t realise so much of their vernacular, so much of our culture is built off of the Australian TV and movie industry.” The 2026 Gold Logie noiminees (from left): Poh Ling Yeow, Allison Langdon, Robert Irwin, Julia Morris, Lisa Millar and Sam Pang. Todd Woodbridge is also a nominee. Getty Images So, can he make the Logies cool again? “For me, the way to make something cool and interesting is to not really try too hard to make it cool,” he says. “Stick to your guns. If you’re doing something that you think is funny and fun and interesting – ‘Oh, this gives me a sense of excitement’ – then you hope that the audience are taking that on board, and you take them with you on that journey. So for me, I want to build a Logies this year that is something I would enjoy.” Related Article Logies Full list of nominees at the 2026 Logie Awards Yes, that will probably include animals and, yes, it will more than likely include a few dance moves. Khaki sequins? “Australia Zoo meets Logies meets dancing. I think you can do it all,” he says. In truth, if anyone was born to do the job, it’s probably Irwin. After all, documentary cameras were famously in the room when he was born in 2003, and he made his first appearance on TV the next year, on Enough Rope with Andrew Denton, with dad Steve and mum Terri. He hosted his first show, Wild But True, in 2014 and, in 2017, he began the first of many appearances on US late-night TV when, as a 13-year-old, he introduced Jimmy Fallon to an African dwarf crocodile.





Irwin is very much following in his dad’s footsteps. Steve Irwin had a rich and colourful history with the Logies, including that time in 2003 when he infamously brought a carpet snake to the awards that bit sports broadcaster Tim Webster on the thigh (“There’s a little bruise there and quite a few little puncture marks,” Webster said afterwards). Steve Irwin was also inducted posthumously into the Hall of Fame in 2007, in recognition of his contributions to wildlife documentaries and television, and his influence will no doubt be felt at this year’s Logies. Steve Irwin on the red carpet at the 2004 Logies at Crown Towers in Melbourne. Robert Irwin with Jimmy Fallon on his first appearance on US late-night TV in 2017. NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Bindi, Robert and Terri Irwin after Robert won the US version of Dancing with the Stars. Disney/ABC “It is definitely the honour of my life to get to continue that,” says Irwin. “And I feel like it’s my job to bring that message to a new generation, to a new audience. Dad presented there, so many people in the room he knew very, very well. Immediately, Rove McManus springs to mind. Every time he would see Rove, he’d pick him up, which I don’t know if Rove liked that or not, but he didn’t really have a choice. So, you know, the people who were friends of my dad and my family are going to be in the room, too. “I definitely feel this is less of a responsibility and more of a joy to be able to go, ‘Well, here I am, sort of continuing where they left off’. It’s going to be an absolute full-circle moment and a real privilege to be part of.” For anyone who has lost a parent, those constant reminders of the loss can be difficult to navigate, let alone on a public stage. For Irwin, that grief is something he has navigated his whole life, a “childhood defined by loss”, as he puts it.



Related Article Opinion

Logies Seven thinks they’ve been snubbed by the Logies. They only have themselves to blame Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “It really matures you very quickly,” he says. “It’s this interesting thing. For me, it meant I sort of gained perspective on the value of life very early on, because loss was always just sort of like inbuilt factory settings. I lost Dad [when I was] two years old, all I’d ever really known was having some sort of piece of me missing, which is very challenging, and it’s always hard to talk about. “But I find I gain something back. I almost gain some form of reconnection with Dad when I do talk about him, when I do see footage of him that I haven’t seen before. When I hear a story that someone shares about him, is it painful? Yes, but I’ve learnt to embrace that, and I’ve learnt the importance of embracing that pain.” With one week to go until the Logies, though, Irwin does have someone else on his mind: his I’m a Celeb co-host, Morris, who has been nominated for the fifth time for a Gold Logie, as well as for most popular presenter. They are both in the unusual position of being nominated for a show that has been “rested” by Ten, and has now been picked up by Seven. And while no hosts have been confirmed for Seven’s version – although the rumour mill suggests the return of Dr Chris Brown – neither Irwin nor Morris have publicly been linked to the show. Irwin and Morris both co-hosted I’m a Celebrity ... Get Me Out of Here!, and are both nominated for the Gold Logie. “It’s very, very bittersweet and obviously, I’m a Celeb has been part of the Channel Ten culture and the Channel Ten family for so long,” he says. “And I think when you’re just doing it, pumping it out every year – I only got to work on it for three seasons, but for Julia Morris it was 12 [years] – when you wrap one season, you’re already starting thinking about the next. There’s 500 people in the crew. It really is a big staple in your life. And I think for both of us, it was the first time we actually got to look back and go, ‘Oh, that was pretty cool, that was awesome what we got to do on that show’.”

World.title: Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalImmigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ Paul Sakkal August 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Coalition has accused Labor of exploiting a $171 million multicultural fund to bankroll its own seats and entrench “ghettoisation” of migrant communities, as the Albanese government quietly shifts funding toward cross-cultural programs over narrower ethnic or religious activities. A clash over border controls and diversity, fed by rising support for One Nation, will heat up this fortnight as parliament resumes and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tries to balance support for migrant communities with public demands to tighten migration. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke and the prime minister are trying to steer a contentious policy package on migration. Alex Ellinghausen After abruptly delaying the announcement of a migration overhaul last week, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is expected to provide more detail in coming days, on a package of new measures to cut the net overseas migration intake to its budget forecast of 225,000 per year. Nine months after the Bondi massacre enlivened debate over social cohesion, Labor is toying with proposals to rework the skills program to better serve the economy, put stricter rules on working holidaymakers and family reunion visas, and cut work rights from visa overstayers. Polls suggest there is support among voters for tighter controls on migration.



As the Coalition prepares its plan to revamp the skilled migration system, they will kick off the week in parliament by campaigning against Labor’s use of grants. The $170 million Supporting Multicultural Communities program flowed at about 85 per cent to Labor seats, which the opposition’s assistant spokesman for infrastructure Ben Small described as an abuse of funds. West Australian MP Ben Small says the government is using the multicultural grants money to fund “ghettoisation”. Facebook/BenSmallMP “Albanese has been caught red-handed dishing out … money taken off hard-working Australians and using that money to fund the ghettoisation of Australia at the exact moment in time when we need to be brought together as Australians,” he said. “You can’t spin these numbers into something that passes the pub test. I’m not suggesting that not a single one of the projects was without merit, but taken together, this is a gross abuse of Australian taxpayer money.”



The biggest winners were the Jewish Arts Quarter in Melbourne in the Labor-held electorate of Macnamara, which received $19.8 million, the Islamic UMA Centre ($11 million, in Sydney’s Labor seat of Banks that was held by the Liberals before the election) and the Federation of Indian Communities of Queensland ($6 million, in the Labor-held seat of Blair). Labor argues that the skew to progressive-held seats was natural given the Coalition had been wiped out in metropolitan areas where the majority of voters from non-English speaking backgrounds live. The Coalition holds nine seats classed as metropolitan by the Australian Electoral Commission, down from 44 after the 2013 election. “This is selective and misleading analysis from the Liberals designed to manufacture a political attack,” a spokesman for assistant minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs Julian Hill said. “Labor makes no apology for investing in communities.” Hill argued that Labor’s spending fitted with Commonwealth grant rules, which allow this type of funding for pre-election pledges. In contrast the Coalition-era “sports rorts” saga related to competitive grants processes, which are more restrictive than election promises. Labor’s Julian Hill rubbished the Coalition attack. Eamon Gallagher



There has been a long-running debate on whether election commitments from candidates should be open slather. Independent MP Helen Haines and constitutional expert Anne Twomey have argued in favour of tightening the rules. Nationals leader Matt Canavan rubbished Twomey’s arguments, saying in 2023 that it was “nuts” to prohibit candidates from making promises to local groups and instead hand power to unelected bureaucrats. Since the 2025 election, Labor has created new guidelines for the multicultural grants program. They emphasise cross-cultural programs rather than spending on programs or organisations that operate for their own narrow purpose. New grant guidelines seen by this masthead use the term “intercultural” rather than “multicultural”. “Proposals that build understanding between communities and build intercultural links across communities in Australia are encouraged,” it states. “How will your activity contribute to the grant program objectives, including if and how it will build understanding between communities and build intercultural links across communities in Australia?” The shift towards “intercultural” funding was made well before One Nation leader Pauline Hanson used a National Press Club speech to call for a monocultural society. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor initially delivered a confused response to Hanson. Former prime minister Tony Abbott declared the multicultural project had failed. Another former leader, John Howard, advocated a middle path of “Australian multiculturalism”, declaring Hanson’s approach “pointless”.



Related Article Opinion

Diversity Tony Abbott recalls a whiter Australia than I do. Menzies rejected his version, as do many Liberals George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general The change on how Labor will prioritise funding puts into practice Hill’s ideas, as expressed in a February speech. The speech, which made headlines at the time, urged progressives to embrace symbols such as the national flag and warned that Labor must do more than promote diversity for its own sake. “Singapore is strongly focussed on building and renewing intercultural and interreligious trust, understanding and communication,” he said at the time. “Done well, intercultural initiatives will resonate with Australians, and over time should foster reduced prejudice and social polarisation, stronger integration and trust between communities and institutions, and greater resilience to hate-based violence and misinformation.” “Diversity alone in modern Australia is not and cannot be a sufficient goal. Successful multiculturalism means: cherishing communal identities; building bridges between diverse groups; and celebrating things we all have in common.” Albanese gave a firm defence of multiculturalism on Saturday in a speech in Melbourne. He said multiculturalism was “part of the bedrock of our future social and economic success”.



“The proposition that we could somehow return to some older, less diverse past is absurd – because that past never existed,” he told the Asian Business Association of Whitehorse. “With the exception of Indigenous Australians, we are a country of migrants or descendants of migrants. People who came to Australia seeking a better life. Maintaining pride in their heritage while being proud and loyal to Australia.” Related Article Analysis

One Nation PM’s tougher line on migration will define legacy in confronting Hanson Albanese is back at work on Monday after a period of leave. Labor delayed a major announcement on migration last week so that a package of changes could be fine-tuned, amid internal questions on the social and economic consequences of certain measures. Abul Rizvi, a former immigration department official and migration expert, said none of the proposals under consideration, reported by the ABC and this masthead, would substantially affect the net overseas migration rate.



He proposed a series of changes that he said would bring the figure down from 300,000 a year to the desired 225,000. They included: abolishing the option of a third year of stay for working holidaymakers, which was created during COVID; introducing an entrance exam for international students; forcing onshore student visa applicants to study in an area of long-term demand for the Australian economy; increasing the minimum salary for skilled temporary visas from $80,000 to $100,000; reducing the humanitarian intake from 20,000 to 14,000, noting settlement services are struggling to cope; “highly targeted” moves to deport some of the 100,000 who overstay visas; abolishing fiancée visas; and raising the minimum age of the partner visa to 25. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: ASX set to rise after jobs report boosts Wall Street; Sunrise Energy in focus after Pentagon deal
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise after jobs report boosts Wall Street; Sunrise Energy in focus after Pentagon deal Damian Troise August 10, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stocks rose on Wall Street and Treasury yields fell after the government reported that employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs last month. Every major index notched a second straight week of gains, which included several fresh records. It marks a strong start to August following several weak months. Wall Street notched another winning week. Bloomberg The S&P 500 rose 47.68 points, or 0.6 per cent, to 7,757.64. That topped the all-time high it set on Tuesday. The benchmark index has been on a record run throughout the year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 151.83 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 54,036.93. That put it just short of the record it set on Wednesday. The Nasdaq composite rose 342.26 points, or 1.3 per cent, to 26,690.62. The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures set on Saturday pointing a gain of 33 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.61¢ at 5.13am AEST. Reporting season heats up this week.



Related Article Critical minerals Pentagon ploughs $560 million into ‘world-first’ Australian mining project ASX-listed Sunrise Energy Metals will be in focus this morning following the revelation the Pentagon will invest more than half a billion dollars in the company’s “world-first” mining project in central western NSW that produces scandium, a rare critical mineral used in fighter jets, spacecraft and other tools of war. The $US400 million ($560 million) loan is intended to expand production at the Syerston Scandium Project near Fifield, south-west of Dubbo, as the US seeks to urgently diversify its supply chain for rare earths. Elsewhere, Iran and Oman remained short of a final deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, although President Donald Trump signalled patience, saying the US could wait for Tehran’s economic suffering to soften its stance. For its part, Iran ruled out direct talks with the US for now, citing what Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described as repeated violations of a short-lived interim peace agreement signed in June.



“As long as the American violation of the Memorandum of Understanding continues and the US does not make amends for its violations, there is no possibility of resuming negotiations,” Araghchi was cited as saying by state TV. Araghchi also said a pact with Oman to establish a shipping route through the strait was “very close.” That didn’t seem to bother Trump, who on Sunday told Axios in a short phone call that the US was now “low-keying it.” On Wall Street, technology stocks, with their big market values, did much of the heavy lifting for the broader market. Nvidia jumped 2.3 per cent and Broadcom rose 1.7 per cent. The bond market reacted more strongly to the weaker signal on the jobs market, which can be seen as allowing the Federal Reserve more time before raising interest rates to fight inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.67 per cent just prior to the jobs update. It was as low as 4.60 per cent before recovering a bit.



The yield on the two-year Treasury, which more closely tracks expectations for Fed action on interest rates, fell to 4.20 per cent from 4.22 per cent prior to the report’s release. It was as low as 4.15 per cent before edging back up. “Although the stock market is likely to welcome the dovish implications of the report, investors should be wary of the future growth potential of an economy where fewer people are working,” said Peter Graf, chief investment officer at Amova Asset Management Americas, in a research note. Overall, the report paints a dimmer picture of the jobs market, which has been one of the brighter areas of the economy amid rising inflation and worries about household spending. It included a revision to the figures for June and May that involved slashing a combined 103,000 jobs from payrolls for those months. The Fed has been holding interest rates steady amid worries about hotter inflation, fuelled by a rise in oil prices because of the US war with Iran. Wall Street expects at least one rate increase by the end of the year, with forecasts shifting for the next meeting. Expectations for a rate cut in September are down to 42 per cent, from 55 per cent and from 67 per cent a week ago, according to CME FedWatch. A weakening jobs market could make matters more complicated for the Fed, which has to balance supporting job growth with fighting inflation. Raising interest rates can help tame inflation by slowing economic growth. A weaker jobs market, though, could become even shakier under higher interest rates as businesses find it more difficult to expand under increased borrowing rates.



Related Article Residential property What happens when crime is no longer paying for our real estate? Wall Street will get several important inflation updates next week. The most closely watched will be the consumer price index, or CPI, which measures costs for consumers. Wall Street expects it to show that inflation in July rose at a 3.4 per cent rate, which would be a slight easing from the 3.5 per cent rise in June. Inflation has held stubbornly above 3 per cent for most of the year. “Today’s weak payrolls print may ease the pressure on the Fed to raise rates at its September meeting, but next week’s inflation data will still likely be the deciding factor,” said Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, in a research note. The jobs report caps a week dominated mostly by corporate earnings and concerns about the ongoing US war with Iran. Corporate earnings for the second quarter are on track for the strongest growth since 2021. Nearly 90 per cent of companies in the S&P 500 have reported their results and analysts expect profit growth of 50 per cent overall. That has helped allay some concerns on Wall Street about whether big gains for stocks in 2026 are justified. Strong profits help support those gains in stock values.



Airbnb jumped 17.4 per cent following the vacation-rental company’s report that showed stronger profit and revenue for its most recent quarter than analysts expected. Oil prices gained ground. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 1.3 per cent to $US83.55 a barrel. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘Smash those Yanks’: Short channels Gary Hall jnr and doubles down on US sledge
World.content:
SportSwimmingSwimming ‘Smash those Yanks’: Short channels Gary Hall jnr and doubles down on US sledge Tom Decent August 10, 2026 — 5:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Los Angeles: In the moments after coming within 0.71 seconds of Lukas Martens’ 400m freestyle world record at Australia’s swimming trials in June, Sam Short flung himself out of the water and launched into a post-race interview on Channel 9. “Can’t wait to go over there and smash those Pommies up and then go over there and smash those Yanks,” Short exclaimed. Sam Short wins the men’s 400m freestyle at the Commonwealth Games. AP Photo/Manish Swarup In a landscape where many Australian athletes are often reluctant to talk themselves up – or are instructed by media managers and coaches to keep a lid on things – Short’s bravado was refreshing as he sent a warning to English and American swimmers that he meant business. But will it turn out to be his very own Gary Hall jnr moment at the Pan Pacific Championships in California which start on Wednesday (Thursday morning, AEST)?



Who could forget the brash American swimmer declaring on the eve of the Sydney 2000 Olympics that his USA men’s 4x100m freestyle relay team would “smash” the Australians “like guitars” on the opening night of competition. What often gets lost is that Hall was actually complimentary of the Australians in the article in which he was quoted. But his prediction was plastered across the front and back pages as he arrived in Sydney, much to the horror of team officials at the time. American swimmer Gary Hall jnr at the Sydney 2000 Olympics. Rod Taylor The story lives in Australian Olympic folklore, with Michael Klim swimming a world record 100m freestyle split as the lead-off leg before Ian Thorpe mowed down Hall in the final metres to consign the USA to their first defeat in the event in Olympic history. Gold medal winners Klim, Chris Fydler, Ashley Callus and Thorpe then played air guitars to an adoring home crowd.



At that very same pool in Sydney, Short laid down his own challenge to his American rivals ahead of this week’s Pan Pacific Championships in Irvine, California, starting on Wednesday (Thursday AEST). “That went down the wrong way, didn’t it,” Short says of Hall’s prediction 26 years ago. Australian teammates (from left) Ashley Callus, Chris Fydler, Michael Klim and Ian Thorpe celebrate after winning gold and setting a new world record in the men’s 4X100m freestyle relay event at the Sydney Olympics in 2000. Rod Taylor “We ended up smashing them in that race, so hopefully the ending’s a little bit different this time. “That story went down in the history books and is still talked about today. It was a tremendous race and happened before I was born. If I come second in a way like that, I wouldn’t be too fussed.”



Short and his Australian teammates arrived in enemy territory last week ahead of the four-day meet in Irvine, a short drive from SoFi Stadium, where swimming will be held at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Fresh off three individual gold medals at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games in the 400m, 800m and 1500m freestyle, plus another victory in the men’s 4x200m freestyle relay, Short has already ticked off the first half of the ambitious statement he made at trials. The Pan Pacs have not been held since 2018, with the COVID-19 pandemic disrupting the traditional four-year cycle. This week’s meet is also the first major international swimming event on US soil since 2010. However, a number of Australia’s biggest names have opted out or are missing through injury or illness, including Cam McEvoy, Mollie O’Callaghan, Kaylee McKeown, Kyle Chalmers and Flynn Southam.



Australia’s leading hopes include Short, Lani Pallister and Meg Harris, but there has been no walking back Short’s quest to trample the Americans in their own backyard. “I want to keep stirring them up a little bit,” Short said. “I’ve trained so hard and you know, it’s not a lie. I really do want to smash them. I want to win, and I want to destroy them.” 400m freestyle gold medallist Sam Short (centre), silver medallist Elijah Winnington and bronze medallist Benjamin Goedemans. Getty Images The Pan Pacs features swimmers from non-European nations, but Australia’s biggest rivals will be the Americans – and for Short, that means US distance superstar Bobby Finke. The pair endured vastly different fortunes at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Short, battling illness in the lead-up, described his campaign as a “failure” after finishing fourth in the 400m freestyle before missing the finals of the 800m and 1500m events.



Earlier that year, Short had said he believed he could break the 400m and 1500m freestyle world records. Finke, meanwhile, stormed to victory in the 1500m freestyle in world-record time and also claimed silver in the 800m. Bobby Finke drew the US level with Australia on seven gold medals when he won the men’s 1500m freestyle at the 2024 Olympics. AP Finke does not race the 400m freestyle, an event Short will start as a heavy favourite to win in Irvine, but the pair will do battle in the 800m and 1500m finals (Thursday and Sunday afternoon, Australian time). Short has posted faster times this year and arrives in strong form.



Related Article Exclusive

Commonwealth Games Australian swimmer loses leadership role after Glasgow drinking session He will not be the only Australian distance swimmer hoping to strike an early blow against the Americans less than two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics. Pallister is aiming to take down US great Katie Ledecky. Her best chance is in the 800m freestyle, an event the American has won at the past four Olympics and seven world championships. “I think we’re just gonna go to another level,” Short said of his Australian teammates.

World.title: Why private schools are asking for your kids’ NAPLAN results
World.content:
NationalQueenslandNAPLAN Why private schools are asking for your kids’ NAPLAN results Catherine Strohfeldt August 10, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Year 5 student Zane Priede felt a weight on his shoulders walking into NAPLAN this year, but father Markus said there was nothing to worry about. “Zane went really well – it was really good to see that he was above average in all his marks,” the father-of-two said. His son “had a good run” in year 3 at their local state primary school, but the family considered the test primarily as a point-in-time snapshot of Zane’s schooling. Zane and Arabella Priede. Catherine Strohfeldt “The schools use it as a bit of a way to score themselves among [each other], but I don’t put too much weight on it,” Priede said.



Zane has continued to achieve strong results in year 5, but he has already started at the school he plans to attend until year 12 – St Joseph’s College, Gregory Terrace. ACARA chief executive Stephen Gniel. Edwina Pickles That means the Milton family has less to worry about than some other Brisbane parents gunning for a place in private or selective-entry high schools, where a child’s NAPLAN results can make a difference to whether they are accepted. As the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority released NAPLAN results last Wednesday, it criticised the use of the test in enrolment processes. “NAPLAN is not a pass or fail test – and it shouldn’t be used as a proxy for school entrance exams,” chief executive Stephen Gniel said.



Gniel urged families and schools to instead use the test “the right way” – as a diagnostic tool. Last week, Education Minister John-Paul Langbroek also criticised what he called “an issue since time immemorial”. “To see those statistics being used inappropriately is something that we don’t encourage, just as we don’t encourage the use of [NAPLAN results] to have league tables for people to assess which schools their children should go to,” he said. Experts worry that misusing NAPLAN places intense pressure on students to perform in the otherwise low-stakes test, to help boost a school’s marketability. At several Brisbane Catholic and independent high schools, a NAPLAN score is also used to boost families’ applications in the highly competitive enrolment processes.





Brisbane Grammar School’s deputy headmaster of teaching and learning, Steve Uscinski, defended the inner-city independent school’s use of the test, outlining its role in enrolment applications as “consistent with its intended purpose and recognised limitations”. “NAPLAN provides a point-in-time indication of a student’s achievement in literacy and numeracy, and is never used in isolation to make enrolment or scholarship decisions,” he said. Deputy headmaster Steve Uscinski defended Brisbane Grammar School’s use of the test in the enrolment process. Catherine Strohfeldt “The school recognises that no single assessment can provide a complete picture of a student’s abilities, potential or readiness to engage in a particular educational environment.” Uscinski said the test was useful because it provided a nationally consistent measure of student progress, and was considered alongside “academic, co-curricular, personal and other relevant information” included in application forms.



Related Article High school The Brisbane high schools where parents are enrolling their kids from birth Inner-west state school parent Lauren Jackson said she knew other families with students as young as year 1 who were already organising tutors to boost their academic performance. “It’s just become this accepted practice all the way through school,” she said. A member of her family who had been through the high school enrolment process treated NAPLAN results as “a big deal”. “She knew moving from a state school into a private school – they want good NAPLAN results,” Jackson said.



“I know when [my son] goes on to a private school, they’ll look at that, but in terms of his actual learning, I don’t think about it at all.” State-by-state and national NAPLAN data was publicly released on the ACARA website on August 5. World.title: The dirt cheap vegetable that could help save your life
World.content:
Tips & adviceHealthy eating The dirt cheap vegetable that could help save your life Chances are you probably already have them in your crisper, but do you know just how good for you the taken-for-granted superfood really is for you? Jack Rear August 10, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Whether in a salad, as a sweet, earthy side dish or as a crudité, carrots are a bona fide staple and very affordable, usually available for around just $2 a bag. But carrots aren’t just a cheap, versatile ingredient – the humble vegetable is a secret superfood, with its health benefits ranging from improved skin, gut and eye heath to a reduced risk of cancer and better sleep. So, what makes carrots so good for you? Carrots with feta William Meppem A good source of vitamin A Carotenoids have caught the attention of nutritionists because the body can break them down into two molecules, which can then be converted into vitamin A.



“You can get vitamin A from meat, but if you’re on a vegetarian diet or you don’t eat meat regularly, it’s important to eat plenty of carrots,” says Dr Kirsten Brandt, a senior lecturer in human nutrition and member of Human Nutrition Research Centre at Newcastle University, who has been studying the health benefits of carrots for 25 years. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Vitamin A is important for supporting the function of the immune system but it also has a role in eye health, particularly preventing macular degeneration, which can cause blindness in old age. “You need a certain level of carotenoids like lutein, which you’ll find more of in yellow carrots,” says Dr Brandt. “If you get absolutely no lutein for a very long time, it’ll affect your eyesight, but you don’t need very much to get the benefit.” Katrina Meynink’s spiced honey and parmesan skewers with salsa verde. Katrina Meynink They are cancer-busting



Many people think carrots can help prevent cancer as a result of their carotenoid content. Carotenoids are the phytonutrients (chemicals that occur naturally in plants) responsible for the red, orange and yellow colour of many fruits and vegetables such as grapefruit, carrots, capsicum, tomato, and pumpkin. Previous research has linked higher levels of carotenoids (which accumulate in the skin) with a lower risk of chronic disease such as heart disease and some cancers, including prostate, colon and stomach cancers. Dr Brandt and her team published research in 2023, which found eating 300g of carrots per week reduced the risk of getting cancer by an average of 15 per cent. However, this is not because of the carotenoids but rather an entirely different compound within carrots called polyacetylene. These chemicals help regulate inflammation and thus prevent cell damage, offering a protective effect against cancer. “People tend to think carotenoids help prevent cancer but it actually seems to be polyacetylenes,” explains Dr Brandt. “If you find a person with a lot of carotenoids in their skin and blood it’s a sign they’ve been eating carrots, but that doesn’t mean the carotenoids are doing anything in themselves. [But] we know that polyacetylenes work because we’ve done studies on them outside of carrots, and they have the same anti-cancer effect.” Good in salads, too: Katrina Meynink’s chermoula, carrot and chickpea salad. Katrina Meynink



Full of fibre Carrots contain some of the highest levels of fibre of any vegetable, which makes them important for digestive health. Fibre also takes a long time to break down, making you feel fuller for longer. “Fibre plays a really important role in supporting the gut microbiome,” explains nutritionist and author of How To Stay Healthy Jenna Hope. “The gut microbiome is a collection of bacteria in the gut, good and bad. By incorporating more fibre into our diet, we feed the good bacteria, which means less space for the bad bacteria. Those good bacteria produce short-chain fatty acids, which are associated with all kinds of health benefits, from improving mental well-being to boosting our immune system, to improving our sleep. “If you have a lot of good bacteria, you may find it easier to eat more healthily – when we have high levels of the bad gut bacteria we are more likely to crave high-sugar and high-fat foods.” Fibre will also slow down the release of sugar into the bloodstream, so if you have a dessert after your big plate of carrots, you’ll get a less intense “sugar rush” and afterwards won’t find yourself craving more unhealthy treats later.



Carrots make a healthy, affordable soup, like Katrina Meynink’s carrot and lentil soup. Katrina Meynink Great for skin health Because carotenoids accumulate in the skin, “there is some indication they have a benefit for people with sensitive skin who are prone to sunburn,” says Dr Brandt. “It’s almost like a built-in sun lotion: the carotenoids absorb the rays from the sun before they can burn you.” While research into the subject is still ongoing, there are some scientists who think eating carrots might help reduce the risk of skin cancer. “I know one researcher who is looking into a gene that makes it more difficult to convert carotene into vitamin A,” Dr Brandt explains. “The gene is more commonly found in people in northern Europe and this researcher’s hypothesis is that this is to keep the carotene in the skin for longer, which prevents skin cancer, helping that gene get passed on in people with fair skin.”



Carrots of different colours are still very good for you. Does the colour of a carrot matter? “In medieval times, carrots were not orange, they were more commonly white or yellow,” says Dr Brandt. “Orange carrots became popular, so now that’s what we think of when we think of carrots, but you’ll get the same benefits from other colours.” While all carrots – purple, red, white, and yellow – taste roughly the same and have the same levels of fibre, they contain slightly different types of carotenoids. “Yellow ones have lutein, which is good for eye health; purple carrots have anthocyanin, which may have a benefit for heart health according to some ongoing studies; while white carrots don’t have pigment so you don’t need to worry about turning orange,” says Dr Brandt. “But honestly, our impression is that most carrots, regardless of colour, have broadly the same health applications.”



Carrots and hummus are a match made in healthy snack heaven. Getty Images How should you eat carrots for the maximum health benefits? “Ideally you shouldn’t peel carrots because a lot of the fibre is in the skin,” says Hope. “Wash them first, obviously. If it’s within your budget, organic carrots are quite easy to come by because they’re fairly easy to grow.” Beyond that, it’s worth eating carrots with a source of healthy fat. “You could cook them with a bit of olive oil, serve them with hummus, or drizzle them with tahini,” suggests Hope. “That will help with the absorption of the carotene and help ensure you get all the positive effects.” Cooking a carrot also helps break down some of the carotenoid compounds, making it easier for the body to convert into vitamin A too. “However, carrots are also a good source of vitamin C and that will destabilise if you cook them, so it’s good to have a mix of cooked and uncooked carrots in your diet,” Hope adds.

World.title: My suburb is a public transport black spot. At least the streets have fun names
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion My suburb is a public transport black spot. At least the streets have fun names John Hughes Contributor August 10, 2026 — 5:00am

August 10, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“McWhere?” people ask when I speak of my home of more than 20 years. We were barely aware of this suburb’s existence until we started house-hunting as our little family grew. Our new suburb gradually filled with young families, settling into homes vacated by empty nesters. Surrounded by Stafford Heights, Bridgeman Downs and Chermside West (West Chermside in my day), McDowall is less than 10 kilometres from the CBD, but feels like 50 when you’re walking your dog through the bushy hills of the Raven Street Reserve. Some folks boast their suburb is the beating the heart of the city, but what good is a heart without lungs? Leafy McDowall is a suburb with room to breathe. I was gobsmacked when I spotted my first wallaby bouncing down our street, only to discover the green hills are alive with koalas, wallabies, possums, gliders, rakali (our own native otter), reptiles and more bird life than you can poke a stick at.



McDowall also has a darker past. In 2000, triple police shooter Nigel Parodi absconded into the Chermside Hills, sparking a massive manhunt. He was found weeks later, deceased. His victims all miraculously survived. Both reserves are also the favourite refuge of stolen car joyriders who dump and run. The polite silence of the night is frequently interrupted by Polair circling the reserves in the infrared pursuit of automotive ne’er-do-wells. A reserved transport corridor bisects McDowall north to south, a remnant of an abandoned 1960s freeway plan. Various proposals have surfaced over the years, but so far, they’ve come to nothing. We remain a public transport black spot – a wedge of commuter sadness that has many residents driving to work or the nearest bus or train (the Ferny Grove line) into town.



This thickly forested corridor demarcates “Old McDowall” and “New McDowall”. Old McDowall nestles between the corridor and the Raven Street Reserve and is a network of streets named, delightfully, after film stars. Whoever chose them had eclectic tastes. There are 1950s greats (Brando Street, Bardot Street, Ustinov Crescent), edgy 1970s actors (Hackman Street, Hoffman Street, Dunaway Street) and pop music legends (Jagger Street, Bassey Street, Sinatra Crescent). There’s even a Kidman Close and a Crowe Close. Most memorable street name? Could have been a contender. Markus Ravik I live in old McDowall, and we’re surrounded by all the Golden Age names: Keaton, Marx, Groucho, Chico and Harpo. As the namesake of a famous director, the irony is not lost on me. My understanding was that Brisbane-born film star Diane Cilento (once married to Sean Connery, not happily) had parents who owned much of the land in McDowall. When the land was subdivided they thought it would be a nice tribute to their Oscar-nominated daughter to name the streets thus.



The internet, however, tells me it was instead the name of the Paramount Subdivisional Estate that inspired the names. Either way, there’s a Cilento Street next to the reserve. Old McDowall has glamorous 1960s and 1970s architect-designed executive residences complete with sunken living rooms, shag-pile carpets and terrazzo in-ground pools. To me as a Kedron boy raised in a rickety Queenslander, a brick house with internal stairs was a sign you’d made it: the homes of doctors, bankers and SP bookies. Old-guard residents have regaled me with stories of Old McDowall’s promiscuous ’80s: tales of hot tub swinger parties, where partners and fondue recipes were regularly swapped. The only swapping done today is sourdough starter kits – as far as I know. The patchwork of properties in McDowall is woven with regular-sized blocks as well as larger acreages. Developers brutally raze, rezone and replant these blocks with grey townhouses of questionable style, dimensions and affordability.



Much of the wildlife displaced from these properties has found its way to the bird-feeders in our garden: rainbow lorikeets, galahs, king parrots, pale-faced lorikeets, possums. We also have some of the largest carpet snakes this side of the Amazon. Related Article Property prices What the median house price buys around Australia now McDowall is a vital link in the Mountains to Mangroves Corridor – a gossamer-thin wildlife corridor linking the D’Aguilar Ranges to Moreton Bay. It has a dedicated North Brisbane Catchments community group which lobbies local and state governments to protect the environment of this ecological gem of a suburb. They are currently fighting an uphill legal battle to preserve a vital koala habitat. McDowall has a little shopping precinct with a Drakes IGA which seems to retain its friendly staff (g’day Bob!) and remains open when all the other chains are closed – making it the place to be seen on public holidays. Twenty-something years since moving to McDowall, we’ve come full circle, and I realise we are now the empty nesters. Both our retirements are rapidly approaching, and when I’m not searching the interwebs for oceanfront, architect-designed beach shacks my more financially achievable search is for something just a bit smaller, on one level with less shag-pile – but still in McDowall.



In the meantime, my faithful dog glances from me to her lead, and back to me, and I know it’s time to lace up my hiking boots and head for the hills. Get alerts on significant breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress
World.content:
An independent report that found just 54 of the government’s 270 promised mental health reforms had been completed was reworked ahead of its publication to credit it with doubling progress on royal commission recommendations. The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission’s original report also had its judging criteria changed, its ratings improved, and its most critical findings removed in the months after it was first presented to the government. The delayed release and reworking of the report has drawn criticism over the stalled overhaul of the sector following the royal commission and raised concerns that the government is undermining the independence of bodies meant to hold it to account. Even the original report’s author, former Commissioner Annabel Brebner, cast doubt over the credibility of the re-worked findings.



“The initial method emphasised transparency of reporting of progress in implementing the recommendations, and the categories used to assess progress reflected this,” she said in a short statement. “In my view, the difference in methodology raises questions about the overall reliability and validity of the assessments made.” Brebner added she had not contacted the MHWC or sought and explanation on why the report’s content had altered so dramatically. The commission’s long-awaited status update into Victoria’s mental health reforms was presented to the government in December 2025. However, it was not published until June 24, 2026, and, during the six-month delay, at least 75 of the independent commissioners’ original 270 status ratings were improved.



A leaked draft of the commissioners’ original report, which was sent to the Department of Health and some key stakeholders, reveals huge changes were made to the MHWC’s assessments to favour the government’s position. Many of the strongest concerns raised in the original draft – including the impact of budget cuts, a lack of evidence to support government claims and the refusal of stakeholders to work with the Department of Health – are also missing from the publicly released version in June. In one example, four of the five sub-recommendations relating to Aboriginal social and emotional wellbeing reforms have been upgraded from “partial progress” in December, to “in place” in July, while the sentence “the 2025-26 Budget did not include funding for further development of these initiatives” was cut from its findings. By the time the report was released the commissioners who wrote the original version had been removed from their positions by an act of parliament, and an interim commissioner, appointed directly by Minister for Mental Health Ingrid Stitt, had overseen its redrafting and public release.



Three senior mental health figures familiar with the report’s delay refused to discuss the circumstances of its rewriting on the record, fearing reprisals from the government and further financial cuts to vital services. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Mental health watchdog muzzled by ‘drastic’ budget cuts “We have essentially lost independent oversight of the royal commission,” one source said. Another accused the government of undermining the commission’s ability to monitor the failing sector, including slashing its 2025-26 budget to 40 per cent below its forecast expenses, cutting its staff from 54 to 27, and hobbling its independence. “The royal commission’s findings were not just about new services, but about improved system governance, outcomes, and culture,” they said.



“To have such a governance body be defunded and demoted before an election, and information withheld by bureaucrats until the minister’s appointee is in control, shows that not much has actually changed on that front, if not getting worse.” It follows revelations in July that a 33-page CFA report, which gave a blunt assessment of the shortcomings in the state’s firefighting capability, was whitewashed after talks with the state government and cut back to 18 pages. An Instagram post from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission on April 28, 2026 - the day an act of parliament eliminated the role of the commissioners, and the day the Department of Health provided new information to allow for the redrafting of their independent evaluation of the government’s mental health system overhauls. The MHWC was established in 2022 to independently monitor and report annually on the Victorian government’s progress of implementing the mental health royal commission’s recommendations. It was headed by four commissioners, including two with lived experience. Work on its latest report was led by Brebner during 2025 before being reviewed by the watchdog’s full team of commissioners and the CEO.



The commission briefed the Department of Health about its findings in November 2025, and asked for a government response so it could be included in the document before its potential publication in December or January. Two sources familiar with those discussions said Brebner and her team grew frustrated at the government’s refusal to provide a response,and agitated to release the report without one, but were blocked by the then commission chair Maggie Toko. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health ‘Serious step backwards’: Furious response from mental health sector to cost-cutting bill On December 4, 2025, the government introduced to parliament a controversial bill to overhaul the commission’s leadership and limit it’s investigative remit - in contravention of the royal commission’s recommendation - paving the way to replace the four independent commissioners with a single commissioner. A fortnight later, on December 16, the MHWC report was sent to staff and key stakeholders to brief them ahead of an possible January release, which was then repeatedly delayed.



Brebner, fellow commissioners and MHWC staff continued to push for the report’s release up to April 27, when the legislative changes came into effect and their positions were eliminated. Toko was appointed interim Mental Health and Wellbeing Commissioner by Stitt. Footnotes in the published report show that just one day later the Department of Health provided the MHWC with a raft of “authorised information”, allowing for the document’s redrafting. Some of those familiar the original MHWC’s original independent assessments said they were shocked at the extent of changes when the implementation status update was finally released on June 24. A comparison of the documents shows while the original report assigned five possible status ratings for progress on each of the royal commission’s 270 sub-recommendations, the published report cut that to just three.



That included the removal of a category titled “limited evidence of progress available publicly”, which had been assigned to 32 cases where no evidence of work being undertaken, other than press releases and other announcements, could be found. Another rating category, “to be assessed later”, was also deleted. It had been given to 26 sub-recommendations in the original report, where the commissioners deemed new programs were too fresh to be assessed in a meaningful way. The changes left three wider ratings remaining - Not Yet Commenced; Partial Progress; and In Place - and saw at least 75 grades from the original report improved in the one published June. Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said the commission had been established to hold government and service providers to account. “The claims that the government re-wrote and delayed a critical report assessing the government’s performance on mental health is a blow for transparency and accountability,” he said.



“Under the legislation the commission is meant to act as an independent body. This means being free from government interference.” “Good government requires independent advice, scrutiny, and accountability. Yet the Labor government has long engaged in the politicisation of the public service, and independent bodies like the commission, which only weakens democracy.” When asked why its assessments changed, the MHWC told The Age that its December 2025 version was “an early, incomplete draft” that had “gaps or inaccuracies” because it had not been provided with departmental information, and was not approved for release at that stage. It said the report was updated when the department’s response was provided, and this information “informed, but did not determine” its findings.



“At the halfway point of the 10-year mental health reform agenda, the commission sought to highlight both – the progress to date in delivering on recommendations since the royal commission, as well as to highlight the important work still ahead, with detail, accuracy and balance,” Interim Commissioner Maggie Toko said. ”It is important that the commission’s reporting provide the community and all stakeholders with an accurate and comprehensive view on the status of the implementation of the recommendations for mental health reform, that conveys the progress to date, and a sense of optimism and continued commitment towards the ongoing work in improving outcomes into the future.” The Department of Health said it had been provided with a draft of the MHWC’s report at the end of 2025, and provided “factual and technical feedback” between December 2025 and May 2026 to ensure it had up-to-date information. “The MHWC is an independent statutory authority – it is responsible for its own reports, findings and assessments, including decisions about content and publication dates,” a department spokesperson said. World.title: ‘I think you can do it all’: Can Robert Irwin make the Logies relevant again?
World.content:
What business does a 22-year-old, who belongs to a generation that barely engages with traditional media, have hosting the most traditional night on Australian TV?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A



“And so now, particularly after doing a lot more on free-to-air television in Australia, now all my mates were excited for the next season of I’m a Celeb or, ‘Oh, that’s so cool, you’re hosting the Logies’. So my job is to bring that next generation into what we’ve all grown up enjoying. Because I think young people probably don’t realise so much of their vernacular, so much of our culture is built off of the Australian TV and movie industry.” The 2026 Gold Logie noiminees (from left): Poh Ling Yeow, Allison Langdon, Robert Irwin, Julia Morris, Lisa Millar and Sam Pang. Todd Woodbridge is also a nominee. Getty Images So, can he make the Logies cool again? “For me, the way to make something cool and interesting is to not really try too hard to make it cool,” he says. “Stick to your guns. If you’re doing something that you think is funny and fun and interesting – ‘Oh, this gives me a sense of excitement’ – then you hope that the audience are taking that on board, and you take them with you on that journey. So for me, I want to build a Logies this year that is something I would enjoy.” Related Article Logies Full list of nominees at the 2026 Logie Awards Yes, that will probably include animals and, yes, it will more than likely include a few dance moves. Khaki sequins? “Australia Zoo meets Logies meets dancing. I think you can do it all,” he says. In truth, if anyone was born to do the job, it’s probably Irwin. After all, documentary cameras were famously in the room when he was born in 2003, and he made his first appearance on TV the next year, on Enough Rope with Andrew Denton, with dad Steve and mum Terri. He hosted his first show, Wild But True, in 2014 and, in 2017, he began the first of many appearances on US late-night TV when, as a 13-year-old, he introduced Jimmy Fallon to an African dwarf crocodile.





Irwin is very much following in his dad’s footsteps. Steve Irwin had a rich and colourful history with the Logies, including that time in 2003 when he infamously brought a carpet snake to the awards that bit sports broadcaster Tim Webster on the thigh (“There’s a little bruise there and quite a few little puncture marks,” Webster said afterwards). Steve Irwin was also inducted posthumously into the Hall of Fame in 2007, in recognition of his contributions to wildlife documentaries and television, and his influence will no doubt be felt at this year’s Logies. Steve Irwin on the red carpet at the 2004 Logies at Crown Towers in Melbourne. Robert Irwin with Jimmy Fallon on his first appearance on US late-night TV in 2017. NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Bindi, Robert and Terri Irwin after Robert won the US version of Dancing with the Stars. Disney/ABC “It is definitely the honour of my life to get to continue that,” says Irwin. “And I feel like it’s my job to bring that message to a new generation, to a new audience. Dad presented there, so many people in the room he knew very, very well. Immediately, Rove McManus springs to mind. Every time he would see Rove, he’d pick him up, which I don’t know if Rove liked that or not, but he didn’t really have a choice. So, you know, the people who were friends of my dad and my family are going to be in the room, too. “I definitely feel this is less of a responsibility and more of a joy to be able to go, ‘Well, here I am, sort of continuing where they left off’. It’s going to be an absolute full-circle moment and a real privilege to be part of.” For anyone who has lost a parent, those constant reminders of the loss can be difficult to navigate, let alone on a public stage. For Irwin, that grief is something he has navigated his whole life, a “childhood defined by loss”, as he puts it.



Related Article Opinion

Logies Seven thinks they’ve been snubbed by the Logies. They only have themselves to blame Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “It really matures you very quickly,” he says. “It’s this interesting thing. For me, it meant I sort of gained perspective on the value of life very early on, because loss was always just sort of like inbuilt factory settings. I lost Dad [when I was] two years old, all I’d ever really known was having some sort of piece of me missing, which is very challenging, and it’s always hard to talk about. “But I find I gain something back. I almost gain some form of reconnection with Dad when I do talk about him, when I do see footage of him that I haven’t seen before. When I hear a story that someone shares about him, is it painful? Yes, but I’ve learnt to embrace that, and I’ve learnt the importance of embracing that pain.” With one week to go until the Logies, though, Irwin does have someone else on his mind: his I’m a Celeb co-host, Morris, who has been nominated for the fifth time for a Gold Logie, as well as for most popular presenter. They are both in the unusual position of being nominated for a show that has been “rested” by Ten, and has now been picked up by Seven. And while no hosts have been confirmed for Seven’s version – although the rumour mill suggests the return of Dr Chris Brown – neither Irwin nor Morris have publicly been linked to the show. Irwin and Morris both co-hosted I’m a Celebrity ... Get Me Out of Here!, and are both nominated for the Gold Logie. “It’s very, very bittersweet and obviously, I’m a Celeb has been part of the Channel Ten culture and the Channel Ten family for so long,” he says. “And I think when you’re just doing it, pumping it out every year – I only got to work on it for three seasons, but for Julia Morris it was 12 [years] – when you wrap one season, you’re already starting thinking about the next. There’s 500 people in the crew. It really is a big staple in your life. And I think for both of us, it was the first time we actually got to look back and go, ‘Oh, that was pretty cool, that was awesome what we got to do on that show’.”

World.title: Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalImmigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ Paul Sakkal August 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Coalition has accused Labor of exploiting a $171 million multicultural fund to bankroll its own seats and entrench “ghettoisation” of migrant communities, as the Albanese government quietly shifts funding toward cross-cultural programs over narrower ethnic or religious activities. A clash over border controls and diversity, fed by rising support for One Nation, will heat up this fortnight as parliament resumes and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tries to balance support for migrant communities with public demands to tighten migration. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke and the prime minister are trying to steer a contentious policy package on migration. Alex Ellinghausen After abruptly delaying the announcement of a migration overhaul last week, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is expected to provide more detail in coming days, on a package of new measures to cut the net overseas migration intake to its budget forecast of 225,000 per year. Nine months after the Bondi massacre enlivened debate over social cohesion, Labor is toying with proposals to rework the skills program to better serve the economy, put stricter rules on working holidaymakers and family reunion visas, and cut work rights from visa overstayers. Polls suggest there is support among voters for tighter controls on migration.



As the Coalition prepares its plan to revamp the skilled migration system, they will kick off the week in parliament by campaigning against Labor’s use of grants. The $170 million Supporting Multicultural Communities program flowed at about 85 per cent to Labor seats, which the opposition’s assistant spokesman for infrastructure Ben Small described as an abuse of funds. West Australian MP Ben Small says the government is using the multicultural grants money to fund “ghettoisation”. Facebook/BenSmallMP “Albanese has been caught red-handed dishing out … money taken off hard-working Australians and using that money to fund the ghettoisation of Australia at the exact moment in time when we need to be brought together as Australians,” he said. “You can’t spin these numbers into something that passes the pub test. I’m not suggesting that not a single one of the projects was without merit, but taken together, this is a gross abuse of Australian taxpayer money.”



The biggest winners were the Jewish Arts Quarter in Melbourne in the Labor-held electorate of Macnamara, which received $19.8 million, the Islamic UMA Centre ($11 million, in Sydney’s Labor seat of Banks that was held by the Liberals before the election) and the Federation of Indian Communities of Queensland ($6 million, in the Labor-held seat of Blair). Labor argues that the skew to progressive-held seats was natural given the Coalition had been wiped out in metropolitan areas where the majority of voters from non-English speaking backgrounds live. The Coalition holds nine seats classed as metropolitan by the Australian Electoral Commission, down from 44 after the 2013 election. “This is selective and misleading analysis from the Liberals designed to manufacture a political attack,” a spokesman for assistant minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs Julian Hill said. “Labor makes no apology for investing in communities.” Hill argued that Labor’s spending fitted with Commonwealth grant rules, which allow this type of funding for pre-election pledges. In contrast the Coalition-era “sports rorts” saga related to competitive grants processes, which are more restrictive than election promises. Labor’s Julian Hill rubbished the Coalition attack. Eamon Gallagher



There has been a long-running debate on whether election commitments from candidates should be open slather. Independent MP Helen Haines and constitutional expert Anne Twomey have argued in favour of tightening the rules. Nationals leader Matt Canavan rubbished Twomey’s arguments, saying in 2023 that it was “nuts” to prohibit candidates from making promises to local groups and instead hand power to unelected bureaucrats. Since the 2025 election, Labor has created new guidelines for the multicultural grants program. They emphasise cross-cultural programs rather than spending on programs or organisations that operate for their own narrow purpose. New grant guidelines seen by this masthead use the term “intercultural” rather than “multicultural”. “Proposals that build understanding between communities and build intercultural links across communities in Australia are encouraged,” it states. “How will your activity contribute to the grant program objectives, including if and how it will build understanding between communities and build intercultural links across communities in Australia?” The shift towards “intercultural” funding was made well before One Nation leader Pauline Hanson used a National Press Club speech to call for a monocultural society. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor initially delivered a confused response to Hanson. Former prime minister Tony Abbott declared the multicultural project had failed. Another former leader, John Howard, advocated a middle path of “Australian multiculturalism”, declaring Hanson’s approach “pointless”.



Related Article Opinion

Diversity Tony Abbott recalls a whiter Australia than I do. Menzies rejected his version, as do many Liberals George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general The change on how Labor will prioritise funding puts into practice Hill’s ideas, as expressed in a February speech. The speech, which made headlines at the time, urged progressives to embrace symbols such as the national flag and warned that Labor must do more than promote diversity for its own sake. “Singapore is strongly focussed on building and renewing intercultural and interreligious trust, understanding and communication,” he said at the time. “Done well, intercultural initiatives will resonate with Australians, and over time should foster reduced prejudice and social polarisation, stronger integration and trust between communities and institutions, and greater resilience to hate-based violence and misinformation.” “Diversity alone in modern Australia is not and cannot be a sufficient goal. Successful multiculturalism means: cherishing communal identities; building bridges between diverse groups; and celebrating things we all have in common.” Albanese gave a firm defence of multiculturalism on Saturday in a speech in Melbourne. He said multiculturalism was “part of the bedrock of our future social and economic success”.



“The proposition that we could somehow return to some older, less diverse past is absurd – because that past never existed,” he told the Asian Business Association of Whitehorse. “With the exception of Indigenous Australians, we are a country of migrants or descendants of migrants. People who came to Australia seeking a better life. Maintaining pride in their heritage while being proud and loyal to Australia.” Related Article Analysis

One Nation PM’s tougher line on migration will define legacy in confronting Hanson Albanese is back at work on Monday after a period of leave. Labor delayed a major announcement on migration last week so that a package of changes could be fine-tuned, amid internal questions on the social and economic consequences of certain measures. Abul Rizvi, a former immigration department official and migration expert, said none of the proposals under consideration, reported by the ABC and this masthead, would substantially affect the net overseas migration rate.



He proposed a series of changes that he said would bring the figure down from 300,000 a year to the desired 225,000. They included: abolishing the option of a third year of stay for working holidaymakers, which was created during COVID; introducing an entrance exam for international students; forcing onshore student visa applicants to study in an area of long-term demand for the Australian economy; increasing the minimum salary for skilled temporary visas from $80,000 to $100,000; reducing the humanitarian intake from 20,000 to 14,000, noting settlement services are struggling to cope; “highly targeted” moves to deport some of the 100,000 who overstay visas; abolishing fiancée visas; and raising the minimum age of the partner visa to 25. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: ASX set to rise after jobs report boosts Wall Street; Sunrise Energy in focus after Pentagon deal
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise after jobs report boosts Wall Street; Sunrise Energy in focus after Pentagon deal Damian Troise August 10, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stocks rose on Wall Street and Treasury yields fell after the government reported that employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs last month. Every major index notched a second straight week of gains, which included several fresh records. It marks a strong start to August following several weak months. Wall Street notched another winning week. Bloomberg The S&P 500 rose 47.68 points, or 0.6 per cent, to 7,757.64. That topped the all-time high it set on Tuesday. The benchmark index has been on a record run throughout the year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 151.83 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 54,036.93. That put it just short of the record it set on Wednesday. The Nasdaq composite rose 342.26 points, or 1.3 per cent, to 26,690.62. The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures set on Saturday pointing a gain of 33 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.61¢ at 5.13am AEST. Reporting season heats up this week.



Related Article Critical minerals Pentagon ploughs $560 million into ‘world-first’ Australian mining project ASX-listed Sunrise Energy Metals will be in focus this morning following the revelation the Pentagon will invest more than half a billion dollars in the company’s “world-first” mining project in central western NSW that produces scandium, a rare critical mineral used in fighter jets, spacecraft and other tools of war. The $US400 million ($560 million) loan is intended to expand production at the Syerston Scandium Project near Fifield, south-west of Dubbo, as the US seeks to urgently diversify its supply chain for rare earths. Elsewhere, Iran and Oman remained short of a final deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, although President Donald Trump signalled patience, saying the US could wait for Tehran’s economic suffering to soften its stance. For its part, Iran ruled out direct talks with the US for now, citing what Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described as repeated violations of a short-lived interim peace agreement signed in June.



“As long as the American violation of the Memorandum of Understanding continues and the US does not make amends for its violations, there is no possibility of resuming negotiations,” Araghchi was cited as saying by state TV. Araghchi also said a pact with Oman to establish a shipping route through the strait was “very close.” That didn’t seem to bother Trump, who on Sunday told Axios in a short phone call that the US was now “low-keying it.” On Wall Street, technology stocks, with their big market values, did much of the heavy lifting for the broader market. Nvidia jumped 2.3 per cent and Broadcom rose 1.7 per cent. The bond market reacted more strongly to the weaker signal on the jobs market, which can be seen as allowing the Federal Reserve more time before raising interest rates to fight inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.67 per cent just prior to the jobs update. It was as low as 4.60 per cent before recovering a bit.



The yield on the two-year Treasury, which more closely tracks expectations for Fed action on interest rates, fell to 4.20 per cent from 4.22 per cent prior to the report’s release. It was as low as 4.15 per cent before edging back up. “Although the stock market is likely to welcome the dovish implications of the report, investors should be wary of the future growth potential of an economy where fewer people are working,” said Peter Graf, chief investment officer at Amova Asset Management Americas, in a research note. Overall, the report paints a dimmer picture of the jobs market, which has been one of the brighter areas of the economy amid rising inflation and worries about household spending. It included a revision to the figures for June and May that involved slashing a combined 103,000 jobs from payrolls for those months. The Fed has been holding interest rates steady amid worries about hotter inflation, fuelled by a rise in oil prices because of the US war with Iran. Wall Street expects at least one rate increase by the end of the year, with forecasts shifting for the next meeting. Expectations for a rate cut in September are down to 42 per cent, from 55 per cent and from 67 per cent a week ago, according to CME FedWatch. A weakening jobs market could make matters more complicated for the Fed, which has to balance supporting job growth with fighting inflation. Raising interest rates can help tame inflation by slowing economic growth. A weaker jobs market, though, could become even shakier under higher interest rates as businesses find it more difficult to expand under increased borrowing rates.



Related Article Residential property What happens when crime is no longer paying for our real estate? Wall Street will get several important inflation updates next week. The most closely watched will be the consumer price index, or CPI, which measures costs for consumers. Wall Street expects it to show that inflation in July rose at a 3.4 per cent rate, which would be a slight easing from the 3.5 per cent rise in June. Inflation has held stubbornly above 3 per cent for most of the year. “Today’s weak payrolls print may ease the pressure on the Fed to raise rates at its September meeting, but next week’s inflation data will still likely be the deciding factor,” said Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, in a research note. The jobs report caps a week dominated mostly by corporate earnings and concerns about the ongoing US war with Iran. Corporate earnings for the second quarter are on track for the strongest growth since 2021. Nearly 90 per cent of companies in the S&P 500 have reported their results and analysts expect profit growth of 50 per cent overall. That has helped allay some concerns on Wall Street about whether big gains for stocks in 2026 are justified. Strong profits help support those gains in stock values.



Airbnb jumped 17.4 per cent following the vacation-rental company’s report that showed stronger profit and revenue for its most recent quarter than analysts expected. Oil prices gained ground. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 1.3 per cent to $US83.55 a barrel. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
