World.title: ‘Smash those Yanks’: Short channels Gary Hall jnr and doubles down on US sledge
World.content:
SportSwimmingSwimming ‘Smash those Yanks’: Short channels Gary Hall jnr and doubles down on US sledge Tom Decent August 10, 2026 — 5:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Los Angeles: In the moments after coming within 0.71 seconds of Lukas Martens’ 400m freestyle world record at Australia’s swimming trials in June, Sam Short flung himself out of the water and launched into a post-race interview on Channel 9. “Can’t wait to go over there and smash those Pommies up and then go over there and smash those Yanks,” Short exclaimed. Sam Short wins the men’s 400m freestyle at the Commonwealth Games. AP Photo/Manish Swarup In a landscape where many Australian athletes are often reluctant to talk themselves up – or are instructed by media managers and coaches to keep a lid on things – Short’s bravado was refreshing as he sent a warning to English and American swimmers that he meant business. But will it turn out to be his very own Gary Hall jnr moment at the Pan Pacific Championships in California which start on Wednesday (Thursday morning, AEST)?



Who could forget the brash American swimmer declaring on the eve of the Sydney 2000 Olympics that his USA men’s 4x100m freestyle relay team would “smash” the Australians “like guitars” on the opening night of competition. What often gets lost is that Hall was actually complimentary of the Australians in the article in which he was quoted. But his prediction was plastered across the front and back pages as he arrived in Sydney, much to the horror of team officials at the time. American swimmer Gary Hall jnr at the Sydney 2000 Olympics. Rod Taylor The story lives in Australian Olympic folklore, with Michael Klim swimming a world record 100m freestyle split as the lead-off leg before Ian Thorpe mowed down Hall in the final metres to consign the USA to their first defeat in the event in Olympic history. Gold medal winners Klim, Chris Fydler, Ashley Callus and Thorpe then played air guitars to an adoring home crowd.



At that very same pool in Sydney, Short laid down his own challenge to his American rivals ahead of this week’s Pan Pacific Championships in Irvine, California, starting on Wednesday (Thursday AEST). “That went down the wrong way, didn’t it,” Short says of Hall’s prediction 26 years ago. Australian teammates (from left) Ashley Callus, Chris Fydler, Michael Klim and Ian Thorpe celebrate after winning gold and setting a new world record in the men’s 4X100m freestyle relay event at the Sydney Olympics in 2000. Rod Taylor “We ended up smashing them in that race, so hopefully the ending’s a little bit different this time. “That story went down in the history books and is still talked about today. It was a tremendous race and happened before I was born. If I come second in a way like that, I wouldn’t be too fussed.”



Short and his Australian teammates arrived in enemy territory last week ahead of the four-day meet in Irvine, a short drive from SoFi Stadium, where swimming will be held at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Fresh off three individual gold medals at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games in the 400m, 800m and 1500m freestyle, plus another victory in the men’s 4x200m freestyle relay, Short has already ticked off the first half of the ambitious statement he made at trials. The Pan Pacs have not been held since 2018, with the COVID-19 pandemic disrupting the traditional four-year cycle. This week’s meet is also the first major international swimming event on US soil since 2010. However, a number of Australia’s biggest names have opted out or are missing through injury or illness, including Cam McEvoy, Mollie O’Callaghan, Kaylee McKeown, Kyle Chalmers and Flynn Southam.



Australia’s leading hopes include Short, Lani Pallister and Meg Harris, but there has been no walking back Short’s quest to trample the Americans in their own backyard. “I want to keep stirring them up a little bit,” Short said. “I’ve trained so hard and you know, it’s not a lie. I really do want to smash them. I want to win, and I want to destroy them.” 400m freestyle gold medallist Sam Short (centre), silver medallist Elijah Winnington and bronze medallist Benjamin Goedemans. Getty Images The Pan Pacs features swimmers from non-European nations, but Australia’s biggest rivals will be the Americans – and for Short, that means US distance superstar Bobby Finke. The pair endured vastly different fortunes at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Short, battling illness in the lead-up, described his campaign as a “failure” after finishing fourth in the 400m freestyle before missing the finals of the 800m and 1500m events.



Earlier that year, Short had said he believed he could break the 400m and 1500m freestyle world records. Finke, meanwhile, stormed to victory in the 1500m freestyle in world-record time and also claimed silver in the 800m. Bobby Finke drew the US level with Australia on seven gold medals when he won the men’s 1500m freestyle at the 2024 Olympics. AP Finke does not race the 400m freestyle, an event Short will start as a heavy favourite to win in Irvine, but the pair will do battle in the 800m and 1500m finals (Thursday and Sunday afternoon, Australian time). Short has posted faster times this year and arrives in strong form.



Related Article Exclusive

Commonwealth Games Australian swimmer loses leadership role after Glasgow drinking session He will not be the only Australian distance swimmer hoping to strike an early blow against the Americans less than two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics. Pallister is aiming to take down US great Katie Ledecky. Her best chance is in the 800m freestyle, an event the American has won at the past four Olympics and seven world championships. “I think we’re just gonna go to another level,” Short said of his Australian teammates.

World.title: Why private schools are asking for your kids’ NAPLAN results
World.content:
NationalQueenslandNAPLAN Why private schools are asking for your kids’ NAPLAN results Catherine Strohfeldt August 10, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Year 5 student Zane Priede felt a weight on his shoulders walking into NAPLAN this year, but father Markus said there was nothing to worry about. “Zane went really well – it was really good to see that he was above average in all his marks,” the father-of-two said. His son “had a good run” in year 3 at their local state primary school, but the family considered the test primarily as a point-in-time snapshot of Zane’s schooling. Zane and Arabella Priede. Catherine Strohfeldt “The schools use it as a bit of a way to score themselves among [each other], but I don’t put too much weight on it,” Priede said.



Zane has continued to achieve strong results in year 5, but he has already started at the school he plans to attend until year 12 – St Joseph’s College, Gregory Terrace. ACARA chief executive Stephen Gniel. Edwina Pickles That means the Milton family has less to worry about than some other Brisbane parents gunning for a place in private or selective-entry high schools, where a child’s NAPLAN results can make a difference to whether they are accepted. As the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority released NAPLAN results last Wednesday, it criticised the use of the test in enrolment processes. “NAPLAN is not a pass or fail test – and it shouldn’t be used as a proxy for school entrance exams,” chief executive Stephen Gniel said.



Gniel urged families and schools to instead use the test “the right way” – as a diagnostic tool. Last week, Education Minister John-Paul Langbroek also criticised what he called “an issue since time immemorial”. “To see those statistics being used inappropriately is something that we don’t encourage, just as we don’t encourage the use of [NAPLAN results] to have league tables for people to assess which schools their children should go to,” he said. Experts worry that misusing NAPLAN places intense pressure on students to perform in the otherwise low-stakes test, to help boost a school’s marketability. At several Brisbane Catholic and independent high schools, a NAPLAN score is also used to boost families’ applications in the highly competitive enrolment processes.





Brisbane Grammar School’s deputy headmaster of teaching and learning, Steve Uscinski, defended the inner-city independent school’s use of the test, outlining its role in enrolment applications as “consistent with its intended purpose and recognised limitations”. “NAPLAN provides a point-in-time indication of a student’s achievement in literacy and numeracy, and is never used in isolation to make enrolment or scholarship decisions,” he said. Deputy headmaster Steve Uscinski defended Brisbane Grammar School’s use of the test in the enrolment process. Catherine Strohfeldt “The school recognises that no single assessment can provide a complete picture of a student’s abilities, potential or readiness to engage in a particular educational environment.” Uscinski said the test was useful because it provided a nationally consistent measure of student progress, and was considered alongside “academic, co-curricular, personal and other relevant information” included in application forms.



Related Article High school The Brisbane high schools where parents are enrolling their kids from birth Inner-west state school parent Lauren Jackson said she knew other families with students as young as year 1 who were already organising tutors to boost their academic performance. “It’s just become this accepted practice all the way through school,” she said. A member of her family who had been through the high school enrolment process treated NAPLAN results as “a big deal”. “She knew moving from a state school into a private school – they want good NAPLAN results,” Jackson said.



“I know when [my son] goes on to a private school, they’ll look at that, but in terms of his actual learning, I don’t think about it at all.” State-by-state and national NAPLAN data was publicly released on the ACARA website on August 5. World.title: The dirt cheap vegetable that could help save your life
World.content:
Tips & adviceHealthy eating The dirt cheap vegetable that could help save your life Chances are you probably already have them in your crisper, but do you know just how good for you the taken-for-granted superfood really is for you? Jack Rear August 10, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Whether in a salad, as a sweet, earthy side dish or as a crudité, carrots are a bona fide staple and very affordable, usually available for around just $2 a bag. But carrots aren’t just a cheap, versatile ingredient – the humble vegetable is a secret superfood, with its health benefits ranging from improved skin, gut and eye heath to a reduced risk of cancer and better sleep. So, what makes carrots so good for you? Carrots with feta William Meppem A good source of vitamin A Carotenoids have caught the attention of nutritionists because the body can break them down into two molecules, which can then be converted into vitamin A.



“You can get vitamin A from meat, but if you’re on a vegetarian diet or you don’t eat meat regularly, it’s important to eat plenty of carrots,” says Dr Kirsten Brandt, a senior lecturer in human nutrition and member of Human Nutrition Research Centre at Newcastle University, who has been studying the health benefits of carrots for 25 years. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Vitamin A is important for supporting the function of the immune system but it also has a role in eye health, particularly preventing macular degeneration, which can cause blindness in old age. “You need a certain level of carotenoids like lutein, which you’ll find more of in yellow carrots,” says Dr Brandt. “If you get absolutely no lutein for a very long time, it’ll affect your eyesight, but you don’t need very much to get the benefit.” Katrina Meynink’s spiced honey and parmesan skewers with salsa verde. Katrina Meynink They are cancer-busting



Many people think carrots can help prevent cancer as a result of their carotenoid content. Carotenoids are the phytonutrients (chemicals that occur naturally in plants) responsible for the red, orange and yellow colour of many fruits and vegetables such as grapefruit, carrots, capsicum, tomato, and pumpkin. Previous research has linked higher levels of carotenoids (which accumulate in the skin) with a lower risk of chronic disease such as heart disease and some cancers, including prostate, colon and stomach cancers. Dr Brandt and her team published research in 2023, which found eating 300g of carrots per week reduced the risk of getting cancer by an average of 15 per cent. However, this is not because of the carotenoids but rather an entirely different compound within carrots called polyacetylene. These chemicals help regulate inflammation and thus prevent cell damage, offering a protective effect against cancer. “People tend to think carotenoids help prevent cancer but it actually seems to be polyacetylenes,” explains Dr Brandt. “If you find a person with a lot of carotenoids in their skin and blood it’s a sign they’ve been eating carrots, but that doesn’t mean the carotenoids are doing anything in themselves. [But] we know that polyacetylenes work because we’ve done studies on them outside of carrots, and they have the same anti-cancer effect.” Good in salads, too: Katrina Meynink’s chermoula, carrot and chickpea salad. Katrina Meynink



Full of fibre Carrots contain some of the highest levels of fibre of any vegetable, which makes them important for digestive health. Fibre also takes a long time to break down, making you feel fuller for longer. “Fibre plays a really important role in supporting the gut microbiome,” explains nutritionist and author of How To Stay Healthy Jenna Hope. “The gut microbiome is a collection of bacteria in the gut, good and bad. By incorporating more fibre into our diet, we feed the good bacteria, which means less space for the bad bacteria. Those good bacteria produce short-chain fatty acids, which are associated with all kinds of health benefits, from improving mental well-being to boosting our immune system, to improving our sleep. “If you have a lot of good bacteria, you may find it easier to eat more healthily – when we have high levels of the bad gut bacteria we are more likely to crave high-sugar and high-fat foods.” Fibre will also slow down the release of sugar into the bloodstream, so if you have a dessert after your big plate of carrots, you’ll get a less intense “sugar rush” and afterwards won’t find yourself craving more unhealthy treats later.



Carrots make a healthy, affordable soup, like Katrina Meynink’s carrot and lentil soup. Katrina Meynink Great for skin health Because carotenoids accumulate in the skin, “there is some indication they have a benefit for people with sensitive skin who are prone to sunburn,” says Dr Brandt. “It’s almost like a built-in sun lotion: the carotenoids absorb the rays from the sun before they can burn you.” While research into the subject is still ongoing, there are some scientists who think eating carrots might help reduce the risk of skin cancer. “I know one researcher who is looking into a gene that makes it more difficult to convert carotene into vitamin A,” Dr Brandt explains. “The gene is more commonly found in people in northern Europe and this researcher’s hypothesis is that this is to keep the carotene in the skin for longer, which prevents skin cancer, helping that gene get passed on in people with fair skin.”



Carrots of different colours are still very good for you. Does the colour of a carrot matter? “In medieval times, carrots were not orange, they were more commonly white or yellow,” says Dr Brandt. “Orange carrots became popular, so now that’s what we think of when we think of carrots, but you’ll get the same benefits from other colours.” While all carrots – purple, red, white, and yellow – taste roughly the same and have the same levels of fibre, they contain slightly different types of carotenoids. “Yellow ones have lutein, which is good for eye health; purple carrots have anthocyanin, which may have a benefit for heart health according to some ongoing studies; while white carrots don’t have pigment so you don’t need to worry about turning orange,” says Dr Brandt. “But honestly, our impression is that most carrots, regardless of colour, have broadly the same health applications.”



Carrots and hummus are a match made in healthy snack heaven. Getty Images How should you eat carrots for the maximum health benefits? “Ideally you shouldn’t peel carrots because a lot of the fibre is in the skin,” says Hope. “Wash them first, obviously. If it’s within your budget, organic carrots are quite easy to come by because they’re fairly easy to grow.” Beyond that, it’s worth eating carrots with a source of healthy fat. “You could cook them with a bit of olive oil, serve them with hummus, or drizzle them with tahini,” suggests Hope. “That will help with the absorption of the carotene and help ensure you get all the positive effects.” Cooking a carrot also helps break down some of the carotenoid compounds, making it easier for the body to convert into vitamin A too. “However, carrots are also a good source of vitamin C and that will destabilise if you cook them, so it’s good to have a mix of cooked and uncooked carrots in your diet,” Hope adds.

World.title: My suburb is a public transport black spot. At least the streets have fun names
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion My suburb is a public transport black spot. At least the streets have fun names John Hughes Contributor August 10, 2026 — 5:00am

August 10, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“McWhere?” people ask when I speak of my home of more than 20 years. We were barely aware of this suburb’s existence until we started house-hunting as our little family grew. Our new suburb gradually filled with young families, settling into homes vacated by empty nesters. Surrounded by Stafford Heights, Bridgeman Downs and Chermside West (West Chermside in my day), McDowall is less than 10 kilometres from the CBD, but feels like 50 when you’re walking your dog through the bushy hills of the Raven Street Reserve. Some folks boast their suburb is the beating the heart of the city, but what good is a heart without lungs? Leafy McDowall is a suburb with room to breathe. I was gobsmacked when I spotted my first wallaby bouncing down our street, only to discover the green hills are alive with koalas, wallabies, possums, gliders, rakali (our own native otter), reptiles and more bird life than you can poke a stick at.



McDowall also has a darker past. In 2000, triple police shooter Nigel Parodi absconded into the Chermside Hills, sparking a massive manhunt. He was found weeks later, deceased. His victims all miraculously survived. Both reserves are also the favourite refuge of stolen car joyriders who dump and run. The polite silence of the night is frequently interrupted by Polair circling the reserves in the infrared pursuit of automotive ne’er-do-wells. A reserved transport corridor bisects McDowall north to south, a remnant of an abandoned 1960s freeway plan. Various proposals have surfaced over the years, but so far, they’ve come to nothing. We remain a public transport black spot – a wedge of commuter sadness that has many residents driving to work or the nearest bus or train (the Ferny Grove line) into town.



This thickly forested corridor demarcates “Old McDowall” and “New McDowall”. Old McDowall nestles between the corridor and the Raven Street Reserve and is a network of streets named, delightfully, after film stars. Whoever chose them had eclectic tastes. There are 1950s greats (Brando Street, Bardot Street, Ustinov Crescent), edgy 1970s actors (Hackman Street, Hoffman Street, Dunaway Street) and pop music legends (Jagger Street, Bassey Street, Sinatra Crescent). There’s even a Kidman Close and a Crowe Close. Most memorable street name? Could have been a contender. Markus Ravik I live in old McDowall, and we’re surrounded by all the Golden Age names: Keaton, Marx, Groucho, Chico and Harpo. As the namesake of a famous director, the irony is not lost on me. My understanding was that Brisbane-born film star Diane Cilento (once married to Sean Connery, not happily) had parents who owned much of the land in McDowall. When the land was subdivided they thought it would be a nice tribute to their Oscar-nominated daughter to name the streets thus.



The internet, however, tells me it was instead the name of the Paramount Subdivisional Estate that inspired the names. Either way, there’s a Cilento Street next to the reserve. Old McDowall has glamorous 1960s and 1970s architect-designed executive residences complete with sunken living rooms, shag-pile carpets and terrazzo in-ground pools. To me as a Kedron boy raised in a rickety Queenslander, a brick house with internal stairs was a sign you’d made it: the homes of doctors, bankers and SP bookies. Old-guard residents have regaled me with stories of Old McDowall’s promiscuous ’80s: tales of hot tub swinger parties, where partners and fondue recipes were regularly swapped. The only swapping done today is sourdough starter kits – as far as I know. The patchwork of properties in McDowall is woven with regular-sized blocks as well as larger acreages. Developers brutally raze, rezone and replant these blocks with grey townhouses of questionable style, dimensions and affordability.



Much of the wildlife displaced from these properties has found its way to the bird-feeders in our garden: rainbow lorikeets, galahs, king parrots, pale-faced lorikeets, possums. We also have some of the largest carpet snakes this side of the Amazon. Related Article Property prices What the median house price buys around Australia now McDowall is a vital link in the Mountains to Mangroves Corridor – a gossamer-thin wildlife corridor linking the D’Aguilar Ranges to Moreton Bay. It has a dedicated North Brisbane Catchments community group which lobbies local and state governments to protect the environment of this ecological gem of a suburb. They are currently fighting an uphill legal battle to preserve a vital koala habitat. McDowall has a little shopping precinct with a Drakes IGA which seems to retain its friendly staff (g’day Bob!) and remains open when all the other chains are closed – making it the place to be seen on public holidays. Twenty-something years since moving to McDowall, we’ve come full circle, and I realise we are now the empty nesters. Both our retirements are rapidly approaching, and when I’m not searching the interwebs for oceanfront, architect-designed beach shacks my more financially achievable search is for something just a bit smaller, on one level with less shag-pile – but still in McDowall.



In the meantime, my faithful dog glances from me to her lead, and back to me, and I know it’s time to lace up my hiking boots and head for the hills. Get alerts on significant breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Hato Hone St John braces for another call spike after record-breaking ambulance demand
World.content:
RNZ national

Hato Hone St John is asking people to avoid calling an ambulance unless they absolutely need one, as it faces one of its busiest days ever.

The ambulance service declared a major incident response on Sunday and activated its Emergency Operations Centre for the first time since Covid-19, citing extreme pressure from seasonal illness.

Saturday was St John's busiest day on record, receiving 2562 calls through 111, a 34 percent increase from a typical day. The service's daily calls record was also broken three times last week.

By Sunday, the ambulance service had received 16,008 calls for the week, breaking a record set just a week earlier.

St John director of ambulance operations Doug Gallagher said they were asking those who could to see a GP or call Healthline to ensure they could respond to patients, including those with life-threatening conditions, who needed an ambulance as quickly as possible.

"Our message to the public is clear. Only call 111 if you have a genuine health emergency, such as chest pain, trouble breathing, or you're not able to wake a person up."

While patients with broken bones, those who had fallen, and those not in life-threatening pain could expect to wait several hours for an ambulance, Gallagher said response times for the sickest patients remained within safe limits.

But he said Mondays were typically their busiest days.

"Often, patients with chronic conditions are trying to manage themselves at home ahead of seeing their GP or primary carer on Monday.

"If they had been able to access primary care through some of the facilities that are available on weekends, that may have prevented their condition from getting to a point where on Monday, when they're being seen by their GP, they're actually needing to have an ambulance called."

He said ambulance staff were under significant strain, and staff were skipping breaks to keep up with increasing workloads.

"It does happen, and we have some quite robust procedures around that and times when we can break a break in order to respond to an emergency, but also when we can't break a break.

"Our staff, because they're driving, do have to meet the requirements of the NZTA [New Zealand Transport Agency] driving rules, which do put in place a set number of breaks."

He said they were having discussions with Health NZ about ensuring the service and its staff could cope long-term.

"We're very thankful for the additional resourcing that Health NZ, our purchaser, has put into the ambulance service in the last four years.

"We are back again talking to them for our next contract for the next four years. Those discussions are beginning, and we're hoping to have things firmed up by early October."

Health NZ community and primary care funding director Martin Hefford said the ambulance system had responded appropriately to the significant amount of need they were experiencing.

"Health NZ supports Hato Hone St John's decision to activate the major incident response to ensure they have the structures in place to manage current high demand.

"Activating the major incident response gives Hato Hone St John a clear national structure for coordinating decisions and resources at pace.

It also supports closer coordination with Health New Zealand.

It said some hospitals' emergency departments [EDs] were also seeing increased demand, compared with the same time last year.

On average, the number of patients coming to EDs was up 0.4 percent last month from July 2025.

"While there are districts experiencing higher increases in demand, the overall picture remains well within our planning expectations and is not unexpected," Hefford said.

"Emergency Departments are busy, as is usual at this time of year. We have winter plans in place to respond to these demands.

"Health NZ are working closely with St John to support patient flow through hospitals and other services and to ensure people receive the right care, at the right time."

World.title: 'How's this going to work?' - Patient advocate horrified at broken equipment in dental clinic
World.content:
Sitting with her head tipped back awkwardly in what looks like a waiting room chair, the dentist's tools in her mouth, Diana Ayling thinks about how undignified it all feels.

A broken dental chair sits nearby.

According to the dentist assessing her, this particular chair - part of the Oral Health Clinic at Auckland Hospital - had been out of action for more than a year.

It was June, and Ayling - a patient advocate as well as a patient - was well into a round of radiotherapy for her third bout of head and neck cancer.

As part of that care, she explained to RNZ, patients were regularly checked by the dental team.

The oral health clinic at Auckland Hospital had continued to carry out oral screening assessments for some patients, despite the lack of chair.

The moment she stepped into the room and saw the broken equipment, Ayling said she thought "well, how's this going to work?"

The resulting check was "not dignified" for anyone, she said.

In a statement, Health NZ said the hospital-based clinic had been closed since March 2025.

Dr Michael Shepherd, group director of operations Te Toka Tumai, said the majority of dental care was now delivered at Greenlane Clinical Centre and other community sites, as well as temporarily using clinic space at the Starship Children's Hospital for adults.

However, it had been possible to continue assessments for radiotherapy patients "safely and effectively without a specialised dental chair", Shepherd said.

Work on a new dental clinic was underway, requiring "significant" investment in new equipment and refurbishment.

World.title: Why older people may be left out of KiwiSaver
World.content:
Kiwis reaching 65 may not get enough support over what to do with their KiwiSaver money, the Financial Markets Authority says.

Head of financial advice Romil Ghelani said it had conducted a review of access to advice this year and one of the most common "advice gaps" was a need for help, as people started to draw down their savings to live on.

"That's one of the hardest financial transitions that someone can make in their life."

He said, while there were products to help, they were not as common as in other countries.

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Ghelani said the whole KiwiSaver system could do more to assist those people.

"You've got the KiwiSaver providers, the banks who are fund managers and then you have financial advisers as well," he said. "There's a whole system of information and advice, but financial advice takes it one step further.

"Professional financial advice is that value-add and, to be fair, these services do exist, but they're commonly catered towards those higher-net-worth clients, who can afford personalised service from the wealth management firms."

He said everyone else relied on a system of information and guidance, "less so professional advice".

"More New Zealanders are going to reach retirement with meaningful savings to manage. That's a good thing, but it also means there's complex decisions that people will have to face and that's an opportunity for advisors to fill that gap."

What are managers doing?

Some of the biggest KiwiSaver providers said they were taking steps to help people who were nearing the age at which they could tap into their KiwiSaver accounts.

ANZ Investments fund management products general manager Sian August said ANZ would contact KiwiSaver members one year before they could access their funds, encouraging them to start thinking about what they would like to do.

"This includes reminding them they can access free financial advice through our ANZ Investment advisers to help them understand their choices and to develop an investment strategy that suits their individual circumstances.

"We contact them again six weeks before their savings become available to remind them about their options, including that they can access free advice, tailored to their individual situation. This advice is available both before and after their funds become accessible.

"People retire at different ages and life stages, so there isn't a blanket rule for how someone should manage their money or what fund they should be in once they turn 65. It's important for people to understand their own appetite for risk and what their goals are for their life after 65."

She said some had a misconception they had to withdraw their money when they were 65, when it could be left there until the time was right.

"They can also set up a regular withdrawal to give them a regular income stream. Some members aged 65 and older keep contributing, either through their salary or wages - if they're still working - or by making lump-sum contributions.

"This can be a good option, if a member doesn't need their money right away."

At ASB, wealth general manager Emma-Jayne Liddy said it recognised KiwiSaver members' needs would change as they moved towards retirement.

She said ASB would also contact people before they turned 65 to let them know about the options available.

"We also offer access to free advice sessions for those turning 65, as well as guidance and tools that help customers understand how different retirement decisions, such as taking a lump sum or keeping funds invested, could affect their long-term financial position.

"Our goal is to help all of our customers make informed decisions about their retirement savings. We are continuing to see more of our members stay invested in KiwiSaver after age 65, so their savings keep working for them, which is great."

Murray Harris, head of KiwiSaver at Milford Asset Management, said it offered free access to financial advisers, as well as digital tools to help people consider what different withdrawal options and scenarios might look like.

"For clients who meet the threshold, additional support is available through our wealth management team."

World.title: The Detail: Our biggest brains on controlling AI
World.content:
Critical thinkers and changemakers looked at the impact of artificial intelligence on New Zealand communities when they gathered in Auckland

Our biggest brains on controlling AI The Detail Download MP3 23m

Artificial intelligence - and how to take control of it - dominated a meeting of some of the country's biggest business and tech brains in Auckland.

On the same day that we heard of an 11-year unemployment high once again hitting young people the hardest, some speakers had brutal messages on how the globe was changing - and not in favour of school leavers or graduates.

"It's a shit show out there in the world," said Rochelle Moffitt, co-founder of the conference 'Revved. Engineering Change'. "We needed to bring the best of the best in New Zealand - the critical thinkers, the changemakers - so that we can really engineer change that we want to see for New Zealand."

A key theme at the Auckland meeting was the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs and communities, the influence of a few "digital oligarchs" overseas and the need for New Zealanders to build its own AI.

Aotearoa was at a point where it needed to make difficult decisions about artificial intelligence, education and technology leader Frances Valintine of academyEX told the room.

"The algorithms and the AI tools of offshore companies with trillion-dollar valuations and zero interest in the implications for New Zealand have slid into every waking hour of our lives," she said. "I get it, my AI, your AI are highly tuned to impress us.

"I could open up my preferred AI on my phone right now and have a conversation with it that would make me feel seen, heard, valued and intellectually supercharged. My AI tells me I have great ideas."

She said it was not a case against AI - New Zealand needed it - but the country had to be deliberate, directional and bold.

"The question was never should we adopt AI? The question is who do we build it with?"

She took the room back to 1987, when New Zealand stood up to the superpowers over nuclear proliferation.

"The people in New Zealand looked across at the existential threat of nuclear weapons and the testing happening in our Pacific backyard, and we said no, not here.

"We banned nuclear-powered and nuclear-armed ships from our waters. We defied the United States.

"We were suspended from ANZUS, and we faced immense political and economic pressure."

She called the decision a "defining moment in our development as a nation. A determined assertion of national sovereignty and self determination."

Now we face another uncomfortable question.

"Which is harder? Our future Aotearoa, New Zealand shaped by global companies, big tech, bigger money and external values, or a future that we actively curate and shape, based on what we want our country to stand for?

"Both are hard - pick your hard."

Julia Pahina, Founder and chief executive of south Auckland's Fibre Fale, had a reality check for "some of the privilege" sitting in the room, planning a bright new future, when a large section of the population still did not have access to the internet.

"Right now, 25 percent of the Pacific population don't have access to Wi-Fi at home. Twenty five percent.

"We are the fastest growing and the youngest demographic in Aotearoa, New Zealand. We are the future of Aotearoa, New Zealand.

"Whilst I love the conversation about AI and we teach AI, we talk about AI a lot in our communities, I think there's a gap between the current reality and the future, and that gap needs to close.

"We need to be solving today's problems, as well as being aware of what tomorrow's to come."

Nyssa Waters, founder of possibl.ai, which helps businesses adopt AI, has been writing a business case for New Zealand to build its own AI.

"Doing it in a way that we control the destiny of it is really the challenge that we're facing right now.

"At the moment, we are bound by the United States and China largely in terms of models, and what that means is they can own our knowledge, own our data, own everything, and turn it on and off whenever we want."

The audience also heard from tech company heads who are keeping their business base in New Zealand and employing young Kiwis.

Kami co-founder and director Alliv Samson spoke of building her education platform from a local start-up to a business with 17 million users.

"We've proven that, hey, you can actually grow a very sustainable, very influential company just being here and having your network out there."

She said it wasn't always easy finding young workers, but she saw more people returning to New Zealand with strong technology and innovation skills.

Welcoming the room of 800 in Auckland, Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Whātua chief executive Rēnata Blair called for bold thinking.

He introduced two rangitahi of Ngāti Whātua descent, who had won a new scholarship in tech and innovation. The purpose was to ensure Māori were not just participants in the future economy, but designers of it.

He said the conference was useful to his iwi.

"I think the partners will come," he told The Detail. "We are a very good - I don't like the word brand - but we are a strong name, an important name to the city."

Education New Zealand head David Downs revealed the story of a young volunteer at the conference, Amelia Dore, who had lost her job a month ago.

"If you need a marketing or an HR person, look me up and find Amelia, and give her a job and let's make it happen," he told the crowd.

Gore-born Dore, 22, moved to Auckland for work, but now she's considering following her friends to Australia.

Conference volunteer Amelia Dore moved to Auckland for work, but is now considering following her friends to Australia. RNZ/Sharon Brettkelly

"Most of my peers are going to Australia and that's really sad," she said. "My family says, "Do what you've got to do", but you don't want to be away from family, from whānau."

Job hunting was a fulltime job and she felt she should use AI more, but she didn't understand how.

"I struggle, because I don't know if anyone knows the right way we should be heading with AI and policies with AI as well. I genuinely have no clue."

Find out in the podcast if Dore gets a job offer.

Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here.

World.title: Two debutants named in All Blacks team to play Sharks, Luke Jacobson to captain
World.content:
Two debutants have been named in All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie's team to play the Sharks in Durban on Wednesday, which will see Luke Jacobson captain the All Blacks for the first time.

Hooker Bradley Slater is set to make his All Blacks debut just days after being called in as an injury replacement for George Bell. He's been named on the bench alongside loose forward Semisi Ta'eiloa, who will pull on the All Blacks jersey for the first time.

Luke Jacobson was the "obvious choice" to captain the team in their second match of the South Africa tour, Rennie said.

"He is highly respected, has a great feel for the game and will lead through his actions.

"On behalf of the whole squad, I want to congratulate Semisi and Bradley on achieving this very special milestone, and I know their family and friends will be incredibly proud," he added.

Ruben Love is back at first-five, having sat out the first match against the Stormers, when Beauden Barrett played in the No 10 jersey. Fehi Fineanganofo, who was not considered for the Stormers game due to illness, has been named on the wing.

Seven players from the All Blacks team that beat the Stormers 38-21 on Friday have again been named in the 23.

Hooker Asafo Aumua, lock Sam Darry, halfback Kyle Preston, and wing Caleb Clarke, who all came off the bench against the Stormers, will start against the Sharks. Prop Pasilio Tosi, who started in the Stormers game, will provide impact from the bench, alongside fellow prop Ollie Norris and loose forward Ethan Blackadder, who get their second bench start of the tour.

Luke Jacobson in action against France in July. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

Timoci Tavatavanawai and Emoni Narawa are playing for the All Blacks for the first time this year.

"The opening match gave the players a real introduction to the way that South African teams play and the Sharks will be no different. With a short turnaround between games, today has been a big day of preparation. There is a lot of excitement in the group, with the majority of the squad about to play their first game of the tour," Rennie said.
